It is currently explicitly labeled **preview-only / not production-ready**. citeturn854072view3turn854072view0\n\n### What Cloudflare Computer actually is\n\nThe easiest mental model is:\n\n> **A persistent filesystem + execution layer for AI agents, backed by Cloudflare Durable Objects, where the agent can choose the cheapest appropriate kind of compute.**\n\nIt is **not** primarily a virtual desktop or a “computer-use” GUI product like an agent clicking around a screen.\n\nThe core object is a **Workspace**. Cloudflare's own README describes the container as full Linux userland, while the Worker backends avoid a container altogether. citeturn854072view2\n\nThat is the core architectural bet.\n\n### The really interesting piece: Durable Objects + SQLite\n\nCloudflare is using **Durable Objects as the authoritative state layer** for the workspace.\n\nThat matters because Durable Objects give Cloudflare a naturally addressable, stateful unit: one logical object can own its state, including SQLite storage. Cloudflare designed SQLite inside Durable Objects so application code and the database are colocated rather than separated by a conventional network hop. citeturn180193search0\n\nFor Computer, that means the agent's “computer” isn't fundamentally a VM with a disk attached.\n\nIt's closer to:\n\n**stateful object → filesystem abstraction → execution attached to it**\n\nThat is a pretty different cloud primitive.\n\n### What you can actually build with it\n\nThe obvious use case is coding agents:\n\n> “Clone this repo, modify it, run tests, inspect failures, fix them, and keep the workspace around.”\n\nCloudflare has explicitly framed its broader Sandbox platform around exactly this agent workflow. Its Sandbox environments have persistent files, terminals, background processes, browser connectivity, snapshots, and secure egress, and became generally available in April 2026. citeturn420010search0\n\nComputer is more interesting because it tries to **decompose that computer into smaller execution units**, rather than assuming every agent needs the full Sandbox/container experience.\n\nOther plausible applications:\n\n**Research agents:** download documents, transform data, create artifacts, preserve intermediate files.\n\n**Data agents:** manipulate CSV/JSON/SQLite, execute lightweight code, occasionally escalate to a full Linux environment.\n\n**Coding agents:** workspace persists independently from compute lifecycle.\n\n**Multi-step agents:** the filesystem becomes a durable handoff mechanism between agent turns or different agents.\n\n**Agent-generated applications:** an agent can create files/code, run them, and keep the result in a persistent workspace.\n\nCloudflare's broader Agents Week strategy makes this much more obvious. They launched Sandboxes, Git-compatible Artifacts, Agent Memory, AI Search, Dynamic Worker capabilities, and workflow scaling as parts of a larger “agentic cloud” stack. citeturn180193search1turn180193search6\n\n---\n\n## The clever bit: this is not really about “computers”\n\nI think the naming is slightly misleading.\n\nThe important abstraction is:\n\n> **“An agent needs a persistent workspace and elastic execution.”**\n\nA normal cloud VM is too expensive/heavy to allocate per agent at enormous scale.\n\nA pure serverless function is too constrained to feel like a computer.\n\nCloudflare Computer is trying to occupy the middle:\n\n**serverless when possible + Linux when necessary + durable state throughout**\n\nThat is why the three-backend design matters more than the filesystem API itself.\n\n### And there is a significant limitation\n\nCloudflare says the current workspace target is roughly **10 GB**, and warns that the container-side filesystem is memory-backed and that FUSE adds overhead for heavy filesystem workloads. They explicitly suggest thinking in terms of **agent-scale workspaces, not full monorepos**. citeturn854072view0\n\nSo this is not meant to replace a serious persistent disk or developer VM.\n\nAnd, importantly, **Cloudflare itself says it is preview-only and not suitable for production yet.** citeturn854072view0\n\n---\n\n# Where it sits versus other agent infrastructure\n\nThis is where I think Computer gets especially interesting.\n\n### Cloudflare Computer vs Cloudflare Sandbox\n\n**Sandbox** = “give my agent a real isolated computer.”\n\n**Computer** = “give my agent a durable workspace and let me choose how much computer it actually needs.”\n\nSandbox is the more mature/general-purpose product. Cloudflare says Sandbox is already GA and can support full development environments. citeturn420010search0\n\nComputer looks more like an attempt to make that architecture **much more efficient at massive agent scale**.\n\n### Cloudflare Computer vs E2B / Daytona / Modal-style agent sandboxes\n\nThose products generally center around giving an agent an isolated machine/container environment.\n\nCloudflare's differentiator is the **tight coupling between durable state and Cloudflare's serverless execution model**.\n\nThe interesting economic question is:\n\n> Can most agent work be handled in isolates, with containers being the exception?\n\nIf yes, Cloudflare has a potentially very compelling architecture for millions of small agent tasks.\n\n### Cloudflare Computer vs browser/computer-use agents\n\nThis is an important distinction.\n\nA “computer-use” agent generally means:\n\n> **See a screen → move mouse → click → type → observe result**\n\nCloudflare Computer isn't primarily that.\n\nIt is more:\n\n> **Read/write files → execute code/commands → manipulate a workspace → escalate to Linux when necessary**\n\nCloudflare also has **Browser Run**, which is a separate product for browser automation. In May 2026 Cloudflare rebuilt Browser Run on Containers to make it faster and more scalable. citeturn420010search6\n\nSo you can conceptually combine:\n\n**Agent + Computer + Browser Run + Workflows + AI Gateway**\n\nand get something much closer to an actual autonomous worker platform.\n\n---\n\n# Why I think this release matters\n\nMy read is that **Computer itself isn't the biggest story**.\n\nThe bigger story is Cloudflare trying to build an infrastructure layer where:\n\n> **the basic unit of cloud computing becomes “an agent with state,” rather than “an application server.”**\n\nCloudflare's Agents Week makes that strategy unusually explicit: persistent compute, agent storage, memory, search, secure network access, inference, workflows, and eventually identity/payment infrastructure are being assembled as pieces of an agent-native platform. citeturn180193search1\n\nAnd the timing is notable: the public Computer repository went from alpha releases at the end of July to v0.1.0 on **August 3** and v0.2.0 on **August 11**. That's extremely fast iteration for a newly public runtime. citeturn854072view3\n\n### My current take\n\n**Technically:** very interesting.\n\n**As a production product today:** too early; Cloudflare explicitly says preview-only.\n\n**As an architectural direction:** potentially significant.\n\n**The killer idea:** not “every agent gets a VM,” but **“every agent gets persistent state, and compute is elastic underneath it.”**\n\nThat is much closer to what I would expect the infrastructure for large-scale autonomous agents to look like.\n\nThe GitHub project is open source and currently has hundreds of forks, so there is already substantial developer attention around it. citeturn264791view1\n\nurlCloudflare Computer on GitHubhttps://github.com/cloudflare/computer\n\nOne caveat on the research: I could verify the **repo/releases and Cloudflare's surrounding agent infrastructure directly**, but Cloudflare's dedicated `cloudflare-computer` blog post isn't currently surfacing reliably in Cloudflare's public blog search index.       "content": "Absolutely. **For a solo AI agency, I think there are several genuinely useful applications—but I would *not* start by adopting Cloudflare Computer as infrastructure for everything.** I'd use it for one specific class of client deliverables: **agents that need to actually create, manipulate, run, and retain files/code.**\n\nCloudflare itself describes Computer as giving an agent a persistent filesystem plus an execution surface, with lightweight isolates and full Linux containers available underneath. citeturn0search0turn0search1\n\n## The opportunity I'd look at first\n\nImagine you sell an agency service like:\n\n> **“We build you an AI employee that handles X every morning.”**\n\nInstead of your agent just returning text, it gets its own persistent workspace.\n\nFor example, suppose your client is a marketing agency.\n\nEvery morning:\n\n**Agent receives:**\n- Google Analytics data\n- Search Console data\n- CRM exports\n- ad data\n- previous reports\n- client brand guidelines\n\n**Agent does:**\n1. Downloads the data\n2. Runs Python/JS analysis\n3. Creates charts\n4. Compares against previous periods\n5. Generates a report\n6. Saves the underlying datasets\n7. Produces a PDF/HTML presentation\n8. Sends the client a link\n9. Keeps the workspace around for tomorrow\n\nThat's a much more interesting use of Computer than simply asking Claude/GPT to write a report.\n\n---\n\n# 5 agency products I'd seriously consider\n\n### 1. “AI Analyst” for SMBs\n\nThis is probably my favorite.\n\nYou sell:\n\n> **Your company's AI analyst — automatically produces your weekly business intelligence report.**\n\nEach client gets their own persistent workspace.\n\nThe agent can:\n\n- ingest CSV/Excel exports\n- query APIs\n- clean data\n- run calculations\n- generate charts\n- maintain historical datasets\n- create weekly/monthly reports\n- investigate anomalies\n- produce recommendations\n\nThe important part is that **the agent can actually work with files and code**, rather than having everything stuffed into an LLM context window.\n\nComputer's persistent filesystem is specifically designed for this sort of agent workspace. citeturn0news3\n\nYou could charge something like:\n\n**€500–€2,000/month/client**\n\ndepending on how specialized the reporting is.\n\nYou don't need 100 clients.\n\n10 clients × €1,000/month = **€10k MRR**.\n\n---\n\n# 2. AI content-production machine\n\nThis is another very natural fit for an agency.\n\nInstead of:\n\n> “AI writes LinkedIn posts.”\n\nBuild:\n\n> **AI Content Department**\n\nThe workspace could contain:\n\n```text\n/client\n  /brand\n  /voice\n  /research\n  /competitors\n  /content\n  /images\n  /analytics\n  /published\n```\n\nThe agent can progressively build the client's content library.\n\nFor example:\n\n**Monday**\n\nResearch competitors → identify topics → analyze performance.\n\n**Tuesday**\n\nGenerate 20 ideas → research sources → create briefs.\n\n**Wednesday**\n\nWrite articles → create social posts → generate images.\n\n**Thursday**\n\nHuman approval.\n\n**Friday**\n\nPublish → record URLs → update performance database.\n\nThe persistent workspace becomes the agent's **memory + working directory + asset library**.\n\nThat is considerably more powerful than a chatbot with a giant system prompt.\n\n---\n\n# 3. AI website maintenance agency\n\nThis one gets particularly interesting with Computer.\n\nYou could sell:\n\n> **“Your website has an AI developer on call.”**\n\nClient gives you GitHub access.\n\nAgent has a persistent workspace containing the project.\n\nThen requests come in:\n\n> “Add this case study.”\n\n> “Fix the broken mobile layout.”\n\n> “Update the pricing page.”\n\n> “Create a landing page for our new service.”\n\n> “Why did conversions drop?”\n\nThe agent:\n\n**Git → inspect → modify → run tests → preview → deploy**\n\nCloudflare's Computer announcement actually gives a bug-triage agent as one of its examples. citeturn0search0\n\nThis is where the **container escalation** becomes valuable: trivial filesystem/code operations can happen cheaply, while tasks requiring a real Linux environment can use the container backend. citeturn0search1\n\nYou could productize this as:\n\n**€500 setup + €300–€1,500/month maintenance**\n\nrather than selling hours.\n\n---\n\n# 4. “AI back office” for a specific industry\n\nThis is where I think the **real solo-founder opportunity** is.\n\nDon't sell:\n\n> “AI automation.”\n\nSell:\n\n> **“AI operations manager for [specific industry].”**\n\nFor example:\n\n### Real-estate agency\n\nEvery morning the agent:\n\n- checks new leads\n- cleans CRM data\n- researches properties\n- generates listing descriptions\n- creates PDF property packs\n- analyzes lead conversion\n- prepares follow-ups\n- updates spreadsheets\n- generates weekly management reports\n\n### Recruitment agency\n\nAgent:\n\n- processes CVs\n- extracts structured information\n- compares candidates\n- prepares candidate summaries\n- generates client reports\n- maintains candidate files\n- creates outreach lists\n- analyzes recruitment pipeline\n\n### E-commerce company\n\nAgent:\n\n- downloads sales data\n- analyzes SKUs\n- detects anomalies\n- creates inventory reports\n- researches competitors\n- generates product descriptions\n- creates advertising assets\n- produces weekly recommendations\n\nThe important distinction is:\n\n**You're not selling an AI chatbot.**\n\nYou're selling an **AI worker with a workspace**.\n\n---\n\n# 5. “Turn any spreadsheet process into an AI worker”\n\nThis might actually be the easiest one to sell.\n\nFind businesses doing things like:\n\n> Download Excel → clean it → calculate things → copy results → make a report → email someone.\n\nThose are fantastic agent opportunities.\n\nFor example:\n\n**Client uploads 12 Excel files**\n\n↓\n\nComputer agent creates a workspace\n\n↓\n\nAgent runs Python/JS transformations\n\n↓\n\nProduces:\n\n```text\nclean_data.csv\nanalysis.xlsx\ncharts/\nmanagement_report.pdf\nrecommendations.md\n```\n\n↓\n\nHuman reviews\n\n↓\n\nClient receives final report.\n\nThat is a **very concrete ROI proposition**.\n\nAnd you can charge based on business value rather than tokens.\n\n---\n\n# The really interesting architecture for a solo agency\n\nI would think about your stack like this:\n\n```text\n                 CLIENT\n                    │\n                    ▼\n             Your AI Agent\n                    │\n          ┌─────────┴─────────┐\n          │                   │\n       LLM/API            Cloudflare\n                            Computer\n                               │\n                     ┌─────────┴─────────┐\n                     │                   │\n                Persistent            Runtime\n                Workspace                │\n                     │           ┌───────┴───────┐\n                     │           │               │\n                  Files       Isolate         Container\n                     │\n                     ▼\n               Client data\n               Client assets\n               Agent outputs\n               Agent history\n```\n\nThe key is that **the LLM isn't the product**.\n\nThe product is:\n\n> **Agent + tools + workspace + workflows + integrations + domain knowledge**\n\nThat's much harder for the client to replace with “I'll just use ChatGPT.”\n\n---\n\n# And there's an even bigger Cloudflare angle\n\nI wouldn't look at Computer in isolation.\n\nCloudflare is currently assembling a pretty comprehensive agent stack.\n\nThey now have:\n\n- **Computer** — persistent agent workspace/execution\n- **Sandbox** — persistent isolated environments\n- **Workers** — serverless execution\n- **Durable Objects** — state\n- **R2** — object storage\n- **AI Gateway** — model routing/observability\n- **Agents SDK** — agent framework\n- **Workflows** — durable long-running processes\n- **Browser tooling** — web interaction\n- **Cloudflare OS** — an open-source agent workspace/application layer\n\nCloudflare's current positioning is explicitly around infrastructure built for autonomous agents. citeturn0search4turn0search26\n\nAnd Cloudflare OS is particularly interesting for an agency because it is now open source and designed around **company context, skills, isolated agent runtimes, internal systems, and persistent workspaces**. citeturn0search15\n\nThat starts looking less like “Cloudflare has a cool new API” and more like:\n\n> **You could potentially build your entire AI-agency delivery platform on top of Cloudflare.**\n\n---\n\n# But here's what I would NOT do\n\nI wouldn't spend the next two weeks learning Cloudflare Computer just because it's new.\n\nIt's currently an **early preview**, so I'd treat it as experimental infrastructure rather than something I'd promise mission-critical client SLAs around. citeturn0search1\n\nAnd if your agency currently builds things like:\n\n- lead qualification\n- email automation\n- CRM updates\n- chatbots\n- appointment booking\n- simple RAG\n- Slack/Teams automations\n\n…**you probably don't need Computer yet.**\n\nNormal serverless functions + APIs + an LLM are simpler.\n\nComputer becomes compelling when the agent needs to **work like a junior employee sitting at a computer**:\n\n> files → code → spreadsheets → reports → assets → iterative work → persistent state.\n\n---\n\n## If I were you, I'd build this\n\nI'd pick **one boring, expensive business process**.\n\nFor example:\n\n### “AI Monthly Reporting Department”\n\nYou approach 20 marketing agencies.\n\nPitch:\n\n> **Give us your client reporting process. We'll turn it into an AI analyst that automatically collects the data, analyzes it, creates the report, and prepares the client presentation every month. A human reviews it before delivery.**\n\nThen behind the scenes:\n\n**Cloudflare Computer**\n\n→ persistent client workspace\n\n**LLM**\n\n→ reasoning/writing\n\n**APIs**\n\n→ GA4 / Search Console / Meta / HubSpot etc.\n\n**Python/JS**\n\n→ analysis\n\n**Computer**\n\n→ files + execution\n\n**Workflow**\n\n→ monthly scheduling\n\n**Human approval**\n\n→ final quality control\n\n**Your agency**\n\n→ €500–€2,000/client/month\n\nThat's a **real business**, rather than “I use AI to do automation.”\n\nAnd once you've built it for one client, you can clone the architecture for the next 10.\n\n### The strategic insight\n\nThe thing I'd be trying to sell isn't:\n\n**“AI automation.”**\n\nIt's:\n\n**“We install a digital employee into one specific business process.”**\n\nCloudflare Computer is potentially a very good primitive for that because it gives the employee somewhere to **work**, not merely somewhere to generate text. citeturn0search0\n\nIf you tell me **what kind of AI agency you're currently running / what services you sell**, I can map this much more concretely into **3–5 actual products you could sell, what the agent would do, what Cloudflare components you'd need, and roughly what you could charge.**",

It can maintain the client's files, run calculations/code, compare against historical periods and targets, investigate anomalies, and produce the actual deliverables.\n\nThe pain is real. Multiple agency-focused sources report that reporting consumes several hours per client each month, with the repetitive work concentrated in data collection, formatting, and narrative preparation. citeturn337963search0turn337963search1turn337963search6\n\nAnd the market is already accustomed to paying for reporting software, which is actually a benefit: **you don't have to educate customers that reporting is a problem.** Tools already exist specifically for agency reporting. citeturn337963search5\n\n### But I would *not* sell “automated reports”\n\nThat's too commodity.\n\nI'd sell:\n\n> **“An AI analyst that prepares your monthly client business review.”**\n\nThe difference is important.\n\nA normal reporting tool says:\n\n> “ROAS was 3.2, up 18%.”\n\nYour agent should say:\n\n> “ROAS increased 18% primarily because Brand Search efficiency improved 31%. Prospecting spend increased 14%, but produced 22% fewer qualified leads. We recommend shifting approximately 10% of prospecting budget toward the two campaigns with the strongest lead-quality trend.”\n\nThen attach the evidence.\n\nThat's where the **agent** becomes valuable rather than just a dashboard.\n\n---\n\n## Why this is unusually well suited to Computer\n\nComputer's useful primitive is the **persistent workspace + execution environment**. That's exactly what reporting needs.\n\nEach customer can effectively have:\n\n```text\n/client/acme\n    /raw-data\n    /historical\n    /analysis\n    /charts\n    /reports\n    /brand\n    /instructions\n```\n\nEvery reporting cycle, the agent works inside that workspace.\n\nIt can remember:\n\n- previous reports\n- historical CSVs\n- KPI definitions\n- client-specific business rules\n- brand/template assets\n- previous recommendations\n- exceptions and corrections\n\nAnd it can use lightweight execution for ordinary file/data manipulation, escalating to a fuller environment when needed.\n\nThat's a much better demonstration of Computer than building another chatbot.\n\n---\n\n# Why I'd choose marketing agencies over SMBs directly\n\nThis is the important strategic distinction.\n\n**Don't initially sell to 100 random businesses. Sell to agencies that already have 10–50 clients.**\n\nOne sale can give you many end users.\n\nSuppose an agency has 25 clients and spends 40 hours/month on reporting.       "content": "Fair challenge. **I wouldn't choose marketing because it's inherently the best domain.** I chose it because it has unusually favorable economics for a first wedge.\n\nBut if you're asking, “Where is Cloudflare Computer *most strategically useful* for a solo AI agency?”, my answer is actually broader:\n\n> **Pick a workflow where the agent has to manipulate files, run tools/code, preserve state, and produce a business artifact—not merely converse.**\n\nMarketing reporting happens to fit that pattern. So do several other domains, and some may be better for you.\n\n### Why I initially picked marketing\n\nThe workflow has four properties I like:\n\n**1. Repetitive and recurring.**\nReports happen every week/month.\n\n**2. Lots of messy inputs.**\nCSV exports, APIs, spreadsheets, PDFs, historical reports, campaign data.\n\n**3. Analysis is more valuable than generation.**\nThe customer wants “what happened and what should we do?”, not just text.\n\n**4. There is an obvious labor-saving ROI.**\nYou can replace hours of analyst/account-manager work.\n\nThat makes it relatively easy to productize.\n\n### But there are better opportunities\n\nFor a solo founder, I'd actually investigate these:\n\n| Domain | Example AI worker | My interest |\n|---|---|---:|\n| **Accounting / finance ops** | Reconcile transactions, investigate anomalies, prepare monthly packs | ★★★★★ |\n| **Property management** | Process invoices, maintenance requests, inspections, tenant communication | ★★★★★ |\n| **Recruiting** | Process candidates, research companies, prepare shortlists, update ATS | ★★★★☆ |\n| **Insurance** | Intake documents, extract information, prepare case files | ★★★★★ |\n| **Legal operations** | Organize case documents, compare contracts, prepare summaries | ★★★★☆ |\n| **E-commerce ops** | Analyze sales/inventory/returns, flag issues, create actions | ★★★★★ |\n| **Marketing reporting** | Aggregate campaign data and produce client analysis | ★★★★☆ |\n\nAnd there's a reason some of these are **more interesting than marketing**:\n\nThey have **higher-value decisions attached to the work**.\n\nA marketing report might save an account manager 5 hours.\n\nAn AI worker that processes 200 invoices, prepares an accounts-payable batch, catches duplicates, and reconciles discrepancies could save considerably more operational labor.\n\n---\n\n# The thing I'd optimize for instead\n\nI'd score potential niches on five dimensions:\n\n**Frequency × labor cost × data messiness × autonomy × consequence of failure**\n\nCloudflare Computer becomes particularly interesting when all five are reasonably high.\n\nFor example:\n\n### Bookkeeping operations\n\nA client sends:\n\n```text\n150 invoices\n3 bank exports\n2 credit-card statements\nVAT report\nprevious month's accounts\n```\n\nThe agent:\n\n```text\ningests files\n   ↓\nextracts data\n   ↓\nnormalizes\n   ↓\nruns calculations\n   ↓\nmatches transactions\n   ↓\nflags exceptions\n   ↓\ngenerates reconciliation\n   ↓\ncreates accountant-ready package\n```\n\nThat's **much more “computer-like”** than a chatbot.\n\nAnd the workspace matters because you want the agent to retain:\n\n- prior reconciliations\n- accounting rules\n- vendor mappings\n- historical exceptions\n- supporting documents\n\nThat is almost exactly the sort of workload Cloudflare Computer is designed to make easier.\n\n---\n\n# My revised recommendation\n\nIf you're a **solopreneur with no existing niche**, I would not blindly choose marketing.\n\nI'd investigate:\n\n### **1. Finance/accounting operations**\nBest combination of recurring workload + high labor cost + document/file processing.\n\n### **2. E-commerce operations**\nVery strong because there are lots of APIs, spreadsheets, reports, inventory data and repetitive analysis.\n\n### **3. Property management**\nExtremely operational and document-heavy, with lots of repetitive workflows.\n\n### **4. Marketing agencies**\nProbably the easiest place to *sell* an initial product because the workflow is familiar and agencies already understand outsourcing/automation.\n\nSo marketing is my **“easy first wedge,”** not necessarily my **“highest-value long-term market.”**\n\nThe bigger question is actually: **what sort of work is your agency already good at selling?** Because I'd much rather fit Computer into a market where you already have distribution than chase the theoretically optimal niche.",

    {
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": "I like it **a lot more than the generic “AI employee” idea**.\n\nBut I would change the framing slightly.\n\n## Don't build a “branding agent”\n\nBuild a **Brand Operating System**.\n\nThe distinction is important.\n\nA branding agent that says:\n\n> “Give me your brand guidelines and I'll write posts.”\n\nis already entering a crowded market. Jasper, for example, now has Brand Voice, Style Guide, brand knowledge, and visual guidelines tied directly into its agents and generation workflows. citeturn323357search1turn323357search2turn323357search3\n\nThat means **“AI that knows your brand” isn't enough of a moat.**\n\nBut there's a much more interesting version.\n\n---\n\n# The thing I'd build\n\nImagine you onboard a company and upload:\n\n- website\n- existing marketing\n- brand guidelines\n- pitch deck\n- product docs\n- customer interviews\n- sales calls\n- reviews\n- founder interviews\n- competitor material\n- existing campaigns\n- visual assets\n- examples of things the founder loves/hates\n\nThe system then builds a **living model of the brand**.\n\nNot just:\n\n> tone = friendly\n> colors = blue\n> audience = SMBs\n\nbut something closer to:\n\n```text\nBRAND\n│\n├── Positioning\n│   ├── category\n│   ├── differentiation\n│   ├── enemy/problem\n│   └── category narrative\n│\n├── Audience\n│   ├── segments\n│   ├── pains\n│   ├── desires\n│   └── objections\n│\n├── Voice\n│   ├── vocabulary\n│   ├── sentence patterns\n│   ├── emotional range\n│   ├── things we say\n│   └── things we never say\n│\n├── Visual identity\n│   ├── typography\n│   ├── colors\n│   ├── photography\n│   ├── composition\n│   └── image-generation rules\n│\n├── Messaging\n│   ├── homepage\n│   ├── product\n│   ├── sales\n│   ├── campaigns\n│   └── social\n│\n└── Evidence\n    ├── customer language\n    ├── winning campaigns\n    ├── performance data\n    └── approved examples\n```\n\nNow you have something much more valuable.\n\n**Every future piece of work passes through that system.**\n\n---\n\n# And this is where Cloudflare Computer becomes interesting\n\nThis is one of the first ideas you've mentioned where I think **Computer actually fits naturally**.\n\nGive every brand a persistent workspace:\n\n```text\n/brand\n  /strategy\n  /voice\n  /visual\n  /audience\n  /research\n  /competitors\n  /assets\n  /campaigns\n  /approved\n  /rejected\n  /performance\n  /experiments\n```\n\nThe agent can continually work on it.\n\nFor example:\n\n**Monday**\n\nResearch competitors and update positioning map.\n\n**Tuesday**\n\nAnalyze last month's content performance.\n\n**Wednesday**\n\nIdentify three messaging opportunities.\n\n**Thursday**\n\nGenerate campaign concepts and visual directions.\n\n**Friday**\n\nCreate production-ready assets.\n\nThe important thing is that **the brand model gets better over time**.\n\nThat's fundamentally different from asking ChatGPT:\n\n> “Write this in our brand voice.”\n\n---\n\n# I think the killer product is actually the feedback loop\n\nThis is the part I'd obsess over.\n\nImagine the system generates 20 pieces of content.\n\nThe client approves 7.\n\nRejects 13.\n\nThree months later, the system knows:\n\n> “This company consistently rejects overly clever headlines, prefers concrete language, dislikes rhetorical questions, and performs better when the product benefit appears in the first sentence.”\n\nThen you incorporate **actual behavior** into the brand model.\n\nNow the system isn't merely following the original brand guidelines.\n\nIt's learning:\n\n> **what the company actually means by “on brand.”**\n\nThat's powerful.\n\nAnd it's particularly defensible because the company's accumulated decisions become proprietary data.\n\n---\n\n# Even better: make the brand engine adversarial\n\nI'd have multiple agents with different jobs.\n\n### Brand Strategist\n\n“What should this brand say?”\n\n### Creative Director\n\n“What should this look like?”\n\n### Copywriter\n\n“How should we express it?”\n\n### Brand Guardian\n\n“Is this actually on-brand?”\n\n### Competitor Analyst\n\n“How are competitors positioning this?”\n\n### Performance Analyst\n\n“Did it work?”\n\nThen:\n\n**Performance → Brand model → next creative iteration**\n\nYou get a loop:\n\n> **strategy → creation → distribution → measurement → learning → strategy**\n\nThat's much more interesting than an AI content generator.\n\n---\n\n# And there's a potentially huge extension\n\n### The AI-brand / GEO angle\n\nWe're entering a world where companies increasingly care about:\n\n> **“What does ChatGPT say about my company?”**\n\nNot just:\n\n> “What does Google rank us for?”\n\nThere is already growing discussion around agents, AI-generated answers, and brands attempting to influence how AI systems represent them. citeturn323357news36\n\nSo your engine could eventually monitor:\n\n**Google → ChatGPT → Claude → Gemini → Perplexity**\n\nand ask:\n\n> “How is our brand currently represented?”\n\nThen:\n\n> “What claims are missing?”\n\n> “Which competitors are being associated with this category?”\n\n> “What narratives are emerging?”\n\n> “What should we publish/change to strengthen our positioning?”\n\nThat's **much bigger than content creation**.\n\nYou're effectively building:\n\n> **Brand intelligence infrastructure for the AI era.**\n\n---\n\n# There is one major strategic danger\n\nI'd stay away from:\n\n> **“AI branding for everyone.”**\n\nToo broad.\n\nInstead, I'd initially pick one very specific customer:\n\n### My favorite:\n\n**Seed–Series B B2B SaaS companies.**\n\nWhy?\n\nThey usually have:\n\n- a founder with strong opinions\n- a partially formed brand\n- inconsistent messaging\n- rapidly changing positioning\n- lots of marketing channels\n- limited internal brand resources\n- an increasing need to produce content at high volume\n\nAnd they actually care about the distinction between:\n\n> “generate content”\n\nand\n\n> **“build a recognizable company.”**\n\n---\n\n# Your agency could sell this as a service first\n\nI wouldn't launch SaaS first.\n\nI'd sell:\n\n> **AI Brand Department — we build and operate your company's brand intelligence system.**\n\nYou charge something like:\n\n**€5–15k initial brand build**\n\nthen:\n\n**€1–5k/month ongoing**\n\nAnd behind the scenes, you're building the reusable infrastructure.\n\nAfter 10 clients, you know exactly what belongs in the product.\n\nThen turn the repeated pieces into SaaS.\n\nThat is a much safer path than spending six months building “BrandOS” and discovering nobody wants it.\n\n---\n\n## My verdict\n\n**Branding engine: 9/10 idea.**\n\n**AI brand-voice generator: 4/10.**\n\n**Persistent Brand Operating System + agents + feedback loop + performance intelligence: 9/10.**\n\nAnd there is an especially nice fit with the thing we were discussing because **Cloudflare Computer gives the brand an actual persistent workspace where its knowledge, assets, experiments, outputs, and history can live.**\n\nJasper is evidence that the market already values a brand-intelligence layer; your opportunity would be to go **beyond controlling generated content into continuously operating and learning the brand itself.** citeturn323357search3turn323357search5\n\nThe version I'd be most excited about is:\n\n> **“Every company gets an AI Chief Brand Officer that remembers everything the company has ever said, knows what it stands for, watches competitors and the AI landscape, and helps every future employee/agent create things that actually feel like the company.”**\n\nThat's a considerably bigger idea than automated marketing.",

          "text": "The important thing is that **the brand model gets better over time**."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's fundamentally different from asking ChatGPT:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“Write this in our brand voice.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "I think the killer product is actually the feedback loop"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "This is the part I'd obsess over."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Imagine the system generates 20 pieces of content."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "The client approves 7."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Rejects 13."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Three months later, the system knows:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“This company consistently rejects overly clever headlines, prefers concrete language, dislikes rhetorical questions, and performs better when the product benefit appears in the first sentence.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Then you incorporate **actual behavior** into the brand model."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Now the system isn't merely following the original brand guidelines."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "It's learning:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**what the company actually means by “on brand.”**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's powerful."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "And it's particularly defensible because the company's accumulated decisions become proprietary data."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "Even better: make the brand engine adversarial"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I'd have multiple agents with different jobs."
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "Brand Strategist"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "“What should this brand say?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "Creative Director"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "“What should this look like?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "Copywriter"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "“How should we express it?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "Brand Guardian"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "“Is this actually on-brand?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "Competitor Analyst"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "“How are competitors positioning this?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "Performance Analyst"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "“Did it work?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Then:"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Performance → Brand model → next creative iteration**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "You get a loop:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**strategy → creation → distribution → measurement → learning → strategy**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's much more interesting than an AI content generator."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "And there's a potentially huge extension"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "The AI-brand / GEO angle"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "We're entering a world where companies increasingly care about:"

          "text": "There is already growing discussion around agents, AI-generated answers, and brands attempting to influence how AI systems represent them. citeturn323357news36"

          "text": "So your engine could eventually monitor:"

          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“What narratives are emerging?”"

          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“What should we publish/change to strengthen our positioning?”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's **much bigger than content creation**."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "You're effectively building:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**Brand intelligence infrastructure for the AI era.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "There is one major strategic danger"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I'd stay away from:"
        },

          "text": "**“AI branding for everyone.”**"

          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Too broad."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Instead, I'd initially pick one very specific customer:"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 3,
          "text": "My favorite:"
        },

          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Seed–Series B B2B SaaS companies.**"

          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Why?"

          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "And they actually care about the distinction between:"

          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“generate content”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "and"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**“build a recognizable company.”**"
        },

          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"

        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "Your agency could sell this as a service first"

        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Persistent Brand Operating System + agents + feedback loop + performance intelligence: 9/10.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "And there is an especially nice fit with the thing we were discussing because **Cloudflare Computer gives the brand an actual persistent workspace where its knowledge, assets, experiments, outputs, and history can live.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Jasper is evidence that the market already values a brand-intelligence layer; your opportunity would be to go **beyond controlling generated content into continuously operating and learning the brand itself.** citeturn323357search3turn323357search5"

      "content": "Yes — **there is real need here, but I would separate “need for brand consistency” from “need for a new AI branding platform.”** The first is proven. The second is still being established.\n\n### What the market says right now\n\n**Brands already pay for brand management.** Canva is positioning Brand Kit as infrastructure for keeping distributed teams on-brand, with assets, guidelines and AI generation tied together. Jasper launched Jasper IQ as a dedicated “brand intelligence layer” covering voice, knowledge, audiences, style guides and visual standards. citeturn172229search0turn172229search2\n\nThat is important validation: **the problem is not imaginary.** Companies already recognize that as content volume grows, consistency becomes difficult.\n\nCanva is even explicitly arguing that AI makes the problem worse: without a usable brand system, AI lets companies produce inconsistent material “faster and at higher volume.” citeturn172229search4\n\nSo there is a genuine problem.\n\n---\n\n## But here's the catch\n\nI don't think a company will wake up and say:\n\n> “We need a Brand Operating System.”\n\nThey are more likely to say:\n\n> “Our sales deck doesn't sound like our website.”\n\n> “Our AI-generated content is generic.”\n\n> “Every employee is using ChatGPT differently.”\n\n> “Our agency keeps getting our messaging wrong.”\n\n> “We have 4,000 pieces of content and nobody knows what's still on-brand.”\n\nThose are the **buying triggers**.\n\nThe product has to solve one of those painful problems.\n\n---\n\n# Where I think the opportunity gets much more interesting\n\nAI is creating a **new brand problem that didn't exist at this scale before**.\n\nPreviously, a company might produce:\n\n- 10 blog posts\n- 5 campaigns\n- 20 presentations\n\nNow you can produce:\n\n- 100 blog posts\n- 500 social assets\n- 50 sales decks\n- dozens of landing pages\n- hundreds of AI-generated variations\n\nThe marginal cost of producing content has collapsed.\n\n**Brand consistency hasn't.**\n\nThat's a very interesting mismatch.\n\nAnd companies are already responding to it. Canva says its customers are using brand systems as an operational tool to let employees create more content while maintaining consistency; it reports examples of much faster content production after formalizing brand systems. citeturn172229search3\n\n---\n\n# The second opportunity: AI changes what “brand” means\n\nThis is where I'd get much more excited.\n\nA brand used to primarily control:\n\n**what humans see.**\n\nNow you also need to care about:\n\n**what AI systems say about you.**\n\nResearch published in 2026 is starting to demonstrate that AI recommendations can influence downstream brand search and site visits. One study found that when an AI assistant recommended a brand, subsequent same-name Google searches and site visits increased relative to matched controls. citeturn172229academia78\n\nAnd another recent study found that AI-generated brand answers are heavily grounded in **third-party sources**: about **86% of observed citations were to sources the brands didn't own**. citeturn172229academia88\n\nThat creates a completely new strategic question:\n\n> **“What does the AI ecosystem believe our brand is?”**\n\nThat's different from traditional brand management.\n\n---\n\n# This is where I think your idea could become differentiated\n\nDon't make the product:\n\n> **“Make everything on-brand.”**\n\nMake it:\n\n> **“Understand, control, and improve how your brand is represented everywhere AI and humans encounter it.”**\n\nThen your engine has three layers.\n\n### 1. Brand memory\n\nIt knows:\n\n- positioning\n- audience\n- products\n- claims\n- voice\n- visual identity\n- approved examples\n- forbidden language\n- competitive differentiation\n\n### 2. Brand execution\n\nIt helps create:\n\n- websites\n- decks\n- campaigns\n- social content\n- sales collateral\n- product messaging\n- creative briefs\n\n### 3. Brand intelligence\n\nThis is the really interesting layer:\n\nIt monitors:\n\n- competitor positioning\n- customer language\n- reviews\n- social conversations\n- press\n- search results\n- AI answers\n- how ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini/Perplexity describe the category\n\nThen tells the company:\n\n> “Here's how you're currently perceived.”\n\n> “Here's where your positioning is drifting.”\n\n> “Here's what competitors have claimed that you don't own.”\n\n> “Here's what AI models currently associate with you.”\n\n> “Here's what you should change.”\n\nThat's much harder to replicate with a generic AI content tool.\n\n---\n\n# Do brands understand the value *today*?\n\n**Large brands: yes.**\n\nThey already have brand managers, creative directors, design systems, governance, DAMs, and brand platforms. Canva's enterprise positioning and Jasper's brand-intelligence work are evidence of that. citeturn172229search0turn172229search2\n\n**Mid-market companies: partially.**\n\nThey understand:\n\n> consistency matters.\n\nBut they may not understand:\n\n> **an AI-readable, continuously updated brand system is becoming infrastructure.**\n\n**Small companies: generally no.**\n\nAnd I would **not** target them initially.\n\n---\n\n# So is the market attractive?\n\nI'd characterize it this way:\n\n**Existing demand:** ★★★★★\n**Existing competition:** ★★★★☆\n**AI-driven new demand:** ★★★★★\n**Customer understanding of the new category:** ★★☆☆☆\n**Opportunity to create a differentiated service:** ★★★★★\n**Opportunity for pure SaaS right now:** ★★★☆☆\n\nThat last distinction matters.\n\nI don't think I'd launch:\n\n> “BrandOS — €99/month.”\n\nI **would** seriously consider launching:\n\n> **“We build and operate your AI-native brand system.”**\n\nThen charge a substantial setup fee and monthly retainer.\n\nYou're selling an outcome that companies already understand:\n\n**better messaging + consistent execution + faster content production + brand oversight.**\n\nThe AI layer is how you deliver it.\n\n---\n\n# One thing I'd be particularly careful about\n\nDon't over-index on **AI search/GEO** yet.\n\nIt's compelling, and the research suggests the channel is becoming commercially meaningful, but measurement is still immature. Recent work shows that different AI models can recommend brands quite differently, and AI visibility itself can be unstable. citeturn172229academia86\n\nSo I wouldn't sell:\n\n> “We'll make ChatGPT recommend you.”\n\nThat's a dangerous promise.\n\nI'd sell:\n\n> **“We'll build a system that continuously measures how your brand is represented across AI, search, media and your own channels—and turns that into concrete brand decisions.”**\n\nThat's defensible.\n\n---\n\n## My honest conclusion\n\n**Yes, there is a real need.**\n\nBut the need is **not** primarily:\n\n> “We need AI-generated branding.”\n\nIt's:\n\n> **“AI has made it absurdly easy for organizations to produce huge amounts of content, and now they need a system that keeps all of that output strategically coherent.”**\n\nThat's a real problem.\n\nAnd I think the **next-generation opportunity is even bigger**: the brand system becomes the context layer that feeds not just humans and marketers, but **every AI agent working for the company**.\n\nThat last part is what makes your Cloudflare Computer idea particularly interesting to me.\n\nInstead of one “branding agent,” imagine a **persistent brand brain** that every future agent—sales, marketing, support, website, research, product—has to consult.\n\nThat starts looking like infrastructure rather than another content tool.\n\nciteturn172229search2turn172229search4",

            "customer language",
            "reviews",
            "social conversations",
            "press",
            "search results",
            "AI answers",
            "how ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini/Perplexity describe the category"
          ]
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Then tells the company:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“Here's how you're currently perceived.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“Here's where your positioning is drifting.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“Here's what competitors have claimed that you don't own.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“Here's what AI models currently associate with you.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“Here's what you should change.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's much harder to replicate with a generic AI content tool."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "Do brands understand the value *today*?"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Large brands: yes.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "They already have brand managers, creative directors, design systems, governance, DAMs, and brand platforms. Canva's enterprise positioning and Jasper's brand-intelligence work are evidence of that. citeturn172229search0turn172229search2"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Mid-market companies: partially.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "They understand:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "consistency matters."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "But they may not understand:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**an AI-readable, continuously updated brand system is becoming infrastructure.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Small companies: generally no.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "And I would **not** target them initially."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "So is the market attractive?"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I'd characterize it this way:"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Existing demand:** ★★★★★\n**Existing competition:** ★★★★☆\n**AI-driven new demand:** ★★★★★\n**Customer understanding of the new category:** ★★☆☆☆\n**Opportunity to create a differentiated service:** ★★★★★\n**Opportunity for pure SaaS right now:** ★★★☆☆"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That last distinction matters."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I don't think I'd launch:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“BrandOS — €99/month.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I **would** seriously consider launching:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**“We build and operate your AI-native brand system.”**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Then charge a substantial setup fee and monthly retainer."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "You're selling an outcome that companies already understand:"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**better messaging + consistent execution + faster content production + brand oversight.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "The AI layer is how you deliver it."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "One thing I'd be particularly careful about"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Don't over-index on **AI search/GEO** yet."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "It's compelling, and the research suggests the channel is becoming commercially meaningful, but measurement is still immature. Recent work shows that different AI models can recommend brands quite differently, and AI visibility itself can be unstable. citeturn172229academia86"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "So I wouldn't sell:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“We'll make ChatGPT recommend you.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's a dangerous promise."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I'd sell:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**“We'll build a system that continuously measures how your brand is represented across AI, search, media and your own channels—and turns that into concrete brand decisions.”**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's defensible."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 2,
          "text": "My honest conclusion"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Yes, there is a real need.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "But the need is **not** primarily:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "“We need AI-generated branding.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "It's:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**“AI has made it absurdly easy for organizations to produce huge amounts of content, and now they need a system that keeps all of that output strategically coherent.”**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That's a real problem."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "And I think the **next-generation opportunity is even bigger**: the brand system becomes the context layer that feeds not just humans and marketers, but **every AI agent working for the company**."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That last part is what makes your Cloudflare Computer idea particularly interesting to me."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Instead of one “branding agent,” imagine a **persistent brand brain** that every future agent—sales, marketing, support, website, research, product—has to consult."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That starts looking like infrastructure rather than another content tool."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "citeturn172229search2turn172229search4"
        }

└── Offers     └── Analytics\n                       │\n                       ▼\n                EXECUTION ENGINE\n                       │\n       ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐\n       │ But I would *not* position it as “indistinguishable human UGC at scale.” That is where the current tech and the market still have important limitations.\n\nHiggsfield's MCP is particularly interesting for your architecture: it exposes 30+ image/video models through one MCP connection, can take text/image/audio/reference footage as inputs, and can generate clips up to 15 seconds and 4K. Its own Supercomputer product is already doing agentic planning, model selection and multi-step video generation. citeturn558425search0turn558425search1\n\n## I think this makes your idea much stronger\n\nThe architecture becomes:\n\n```text\n                    MARKETING OS\n                         │\n                ┌────────┴────────┐\n                │                 │\n           BRAND BRAIN       MARKETING BRAIN\n                │                 │\n                └────────┬────────┘\n                         │\n                  CONTENT ENGINE\n                         │\n        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐\n        │                │                │\n      Copy             Images          Video\n        │                │                │\n        │                │        Higgsfield MCP\n        │                │                │\n        └────────────────┴────────────────┘\n                         │\n                    DISTRIBUTION\n                         │\n              Instagram / TikTok / Meta\n                         │\n                    PERFORMANCE\n                         │\n                         ▼\n                  LEARNING LOOP\n```\n\nThe important thing is that the **brand/strategy layer writes the creative brief**, and the video agent executes it.\n\nSo rather than:\n\n> “Make me a Reel.”\n\nyou get:\n\n> “We need 5 creatives aimed at 30–45-year-old founders who don't trust traditional agencies. Give me three hooks, two visual concepts, and five variations of the strongest concept.”\n\nThe system can then generate, score, revise, and package them.\n\nThat's much more valuable.\n\n---\n\n# Is AI UGC actually good enough?\n\n### For some categories: yes.\n\nThe current generation of video models can already produce surprisingly convincing short-form clips, especially when you constrain the task.\n\nHiggsfield supports reference images, identity consistency, video-to-video, first/last-frame control, and multiple underlying models, which gives an agent much more control than simply prompting a single text-to-video model. citeturn558425search5turn558425search4\n\nAnd there is growing real-world use of AI-generated UGC-style advertising. citeturn558425reddit49turn558425reddit54\n\n### But “good video” and “good UGC” aren't the same thing.\n\nThis is the crucial distinction.\n\nA beautiful AI video:\n\n> perfectly lit woman walking through a gorgeous apartment\n\nmay be **terrible UGC**.\n\nUGC works because it feels:\n\n- personal\n- imperfect\n- specific\n- immediate\n- native to the platform\n- emotionally creates:\n\n**10 hooks × 3 concepts × 3 openings = 90 creatives**\n\nThen the marketing system watches performance and learns:\n\n> Hook A wins with women 25–34.\n\n> Product demonstration beats testimonial.\n\n> 0–2 second visual with product close-up beats talking head.\n\n> Founder-style voiceover outperforms polished narration.\n\nNow the AI isn't trying to **replace creators**.\n\nIt's trying to **discover winning creative**.\n\nThat's a much more defensible product.\n\n---\n\n# And that makes the Higgsfield MCP extremely useful\n\nYour agent can effectively treat Higgsfield as its **creative production department**.\n\nIt can say:\n\n> Create a 9:16 Reel based on this creative brief.\n\nHiggsfield generates the shots.\n\nThen your system can:\n\n**select → regenerate → edit → add captions → create variants → export**\n\nThe interesting part is that your agent decides **which model/tool to use**, rather than hard-coding one model.\n\nHiggsfield's MCP explicitly exposes multiple video/image models through a common interface, which is exactly the sort of abstraction an orchestrating agent benefits from. citeturn558425search0\n\n---\n\n# I would give the system a “creative director”\n\nThis is where your Marketing OS becomes genuinely interesting.\n\nBefore generating anything:\n\n### Creative Director Agent\n\nReads:\n\n- brand\n- audience\n- product\n- previous creative\n- performance data\n- current campaign\n- competitor activity\n\nThen produces:\n\n```text\nCAMPAIGN: Product launch\n\nCONCEPT 1\nHook: \"You're probably wasting money the **Brand Guardian** evaluates the resulting assets.\n\nThen the **Performance Agent** learns from the results.\n\nThat creates the full loop.\n\n---\n\n# What I think is possible today\n\n### recording + face cam”**\n\n**“casual testimonial”**\n\n**“day-in-the-life”**\n\nThe goal is not maximum visual fidelity.\n\nIt's **platform-native believability**.\n\n---\n\n# Where I think the campaign history\n- creative assets\n- brand context\n- raw performance data\n- scripts\n- research\n- experiments\n- generated outputs\n\nrather than relying on a stateless API call.\n\n---\n\n## The key product insight\n\nI would **not** compete with Higgsfield.\n\nI would make Higgsfield **one of your creative execution       "content": "Yes — **€15k/month is a very plausible target for this**, but I would *not* think of it as “is there enough market for my software?” yet.\n\nI’d think:\n\n> **Can I get 5–8 businesses to pay me €2–4k/month for an AI marketing department?**\n\nI think the answer is **yes**. The harder question is whether you can make the offer sufficiently differentiated that they choose you instead of Jasper, HubSpot, an agency, or just ChatGPT + Canva.\n\nThere is clearly money in the category. Jasper is already selling business marketing infrastructure with agents, brand intelligence, workflows, API/MCP access and custom pricing; it says more than 100,000 businesses use the product. citeturn526194search0turn526194search1 Zeta Global, meanwhile, is a large-scale AI marketing platform with 2026 revenue guidance around $1.8B, showing the broader market for AI-driven marketing infrastructure is substantial. citeturn526194news49\n\nBut that's actually **good news and bad news**.\n\n### The good news\n\nYou don't need to capture “the AI marketing market.”\n\nYou need:\n\n**5 clients × €3k = €15k MRR**\n\nor\n\n**8 clients × €1.9k = €15.2k MRR**\n\nor even:\n\n**3 clients × €5k = €15k MRR**\n\nFor a solo agency, that is a tiny customer count.\n\nAnd there is evidence that businesses are already paying thousands per month for bundled AI/marketing services; recent agency discussions show €2k/month retainers being used for packages combining AI-generated creative, paid ads, CRM/lead response and automation. Those aren't authoritative market averages, but they are useful evidence that the price point itself isn't absurd. citeturn526194reddit54turn526194reddit57\n\n### The bad news\n\n**“AI Marketing OS” is not enough of a reason to buy.**\n\nThe market is rapidly filling with AI marketing platforms.\n\nJasper already offers:\n\n- agents\n- brand voice\n- knowledge\n- audiences\n- campaign workflows\n- research\n- GEO\n- API\n- MCP\n- custom agents\n\nand its business product is explicitly designed for larger marketing teams. citeturn526194search0\n\nSo I'd be very wary of spending months building a generic SaaS dashboard.\n\n---\n\n# The opportunity I see for you\n\nI'd make the product much closer to:\n\n> **“We run your marketing department with AI.”**\n\nNot:\n\n> “Here is an AI marketing platform.”\n\nAnd **content generation should absolutely be inside it.**\n\nYour stack would look something like:\n\n```text\n                    AI MARKETING DEPARTMENT\n                             │\n          ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐\n          │                  │                  │\n       STRATEGY             BRAND            ANALYTICS\n          │                  │                  │\n          └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘\n                             │\n                     CREATIVE ENGINE\n                             │\n             ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐\n             │               │               │\n           Copy            Images           Video\n                                             │\n                                       Higgsfield MCP\n                                             │\n                                             ▼\n                                        Reels/Ads\n                             │\n                             ▼\n                       DISTRIBUTION\n                             │\n                             ▼\n                       PERFORMANCE\n                             │\n                             ▼\n                          LEARNING\n                             │\n                             └──────→ next campaign\n```\n\nThat is a **very different business** from selling content generation.\n\n---\n\n# Where I'd put the €15k target\n\nI would **not** try to make €15k from 150 customers paying €100.\n\nI'd go deliberately high-touch:\n\n### Offer\n\n**AI Marketing Department**\n\n**€3,000/month**\n\nIncludes:\n\n- brand intelligence\n- monthly marketing strategy\n- social content\n- short-form video\n- landing pages\n- campaign concepts\n- competitor monitoring\n- analytics/reporting\n- ongoing creative testing\n- human review\n\nThen:\n\n**5 clients = €15k MRR**\n\nYou don't need sophisticated SaaS economics yet.\n\nYou're essentially selling **a fractional marketing department powered by software**.\n\nAnd that's strategically attractive because you can discover which 20% of the system actually generates 80% of the value.\n\n---\n\n# The part I'd be most excited about: creative testing\n\nI actually think this could be your wedge.\n\nNot:\n\n> “We'll make you 30 AI Reels.”\n\nThat's becoming commodity.\n\nInstead:\n\n> **“Every month, our AI creative department produces and tests new creative angles for your business.”**\n\nThe system might generate:\n\n**10 hooks**\n\n× **5 concepts**\n\n× **3 formats**\n\n= **150 possible creatives**\n\nBut only deploy 15.\n\nIt observes:\n\n- hook performance\n- watch time\n- CTR\n- conversion\n- audience\n- format\n- visual style\n- CTA\n\nThen the next batch is informed by those results.\n\nThat creates a **data flywheel**.\n\nAnd it fits beautifully with your Computer idea because the workspace retains the actual creative history rather than starting from zero each time.\n\nThere's also strong evidence that the broader industry is moving toward exactly this kind of agentic marketing: current platforms are increasingly connecting strategy, creation, distribution and optimization rather than selling isolated AI features. citeturn526194news48turn526194news50\n\n---\n\n# Would €15k/month be “comfortable”?\n\nHere's my honest answer:\n\n**Revenue-wise: yes.**\n\n**Business-wise: not automatically.**\n\nYou could absolutely get to €15k MRR with 5–8 clients.\n\nThe danger is building something so custom that you're actually running a traditional agency with AI hidden underneath.\n\nYou want:\n\n**Client 1**\n\n→ build manually\n\n**Client 2**\n\n→ notice repeated pattern\n\n**Client 3**\n\n→ productize it\n\n**Client 4**\n\n→ automate it\n\n**Client 5**\n\n→ now your margins start exploding\n\nEventually you want the same underlying Marketing Computer running across clients.\n\n---\n\n# The niche matters enormously\n\nI would **not** target “businesses.”\n\nI'd choose one customer where content is extremely important and there is enough money behind acquisition.\n\nMy first candidates:\n\n**B2B SaaS**\n\n**DTC/e-commerce**\n\n**Info/education businesses**\n\n**High-ticket professional services**\n\n**Consumer subscription brands**\n\nOf these, I'd personally investigate **DTC/e-commerce first if your Reel/UGC engine is central**.\n\nWhy?\n\nBecause a €3k/month marketing system can plausibly be a rounding error against their paid-media spend.\n\nIf a brand is spending €30k/month on Meta/TikTok and you can materially improve creative iteration, €3k for the system is easy to understand.\n\nFor a €2k/month local business, you're trying to justify the same technology against a much smaller marketing budget.\n\n---\n\n# My biggest strategic recommendation\n\n**Don't sell AI. Sell throughput + learning.**\n\nSomething like:\n\n> **“Every month, your AI marketing department researches your market, develops new creative, produces 30–50 campaign assets, launches tests, analyzes the results, and feeds the winners back into your brand system.”**\n\nThat is something a founder can understand.\n\nAnd suddenly Higgsfield isn't the product.\n\nCloudflare Computer isn't the product.\n\nYour LLM isn't the product.\n\nThe product is:\n\n> **a continuously operating marketing machine.**\n\nThat is the version where I think **€15k/month is very realistic**, provided you can demonstrate actual business outcomes and keep a human in the loop initially.\n\nThe next thing I'd do before writing much code is **validate the €3k/month offer with 15–20 target businesses**.         },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "The niche matters enormously"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I would **not** target “businesses.”"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "I'd choose one customer where content is extremely important and there is enough money behind acquisition."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "My first candidates:"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**B2B SaaS**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**DTC/e-commerce**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Info/education businesses**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**High-ticket professional services**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Consumer subscription brands**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Of these, I'd personally investigate **DTC/e-commerce first if your Reel/UGC engine is central**."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Why?"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Because a €3k/month marketing system can plausibly be a rounding error against their paid-media spend."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "If a brand is spending €30k/month on Meta/TikTok and you can materially improve creative iteration, €3k for the system is easy to understand."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "For a €2k/month local business, you're trying to justify the same technology against a much smaller marketing budget."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "---"
        },
        {
          "type": "heading",
          "level": 1,
          "text": "My biggest strategic recommendation"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "**Don't sell AI. Sell throughput + learning.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Something like:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**“Every month, your AI marketing department researches your market, develops new creative, produces 30–50 campaign assets, launches tests, analyzes the results, and feeds the winners back into your brand system.”**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That is something a founder can understand."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "And suddenly Higgsfield isn't the product."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Cloudflare Computer isn't the product."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "Your LLM isn't the product."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "The product is:"
        },
        {
          "type": "blockquote",
          "text": "**a continuously operating marketing machine.**"
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "That is the version where I think **€15k/month is very realistic**, provided you can demonstrate actual business outcomes and keep a human in the loop initially."
        },
        {
          "type": "paragraph",
          "text": "The next thing I'd do before writing much code is **validate the €3k/month offer with 15–20 target businesses**. That will tell you much more than another month of technical research."
        }

      "blocks": [

          "text": "The good news is that the **infrastructure itself is cheap compared with the €15k revenue target**. The cost center I’d watch closely is video generation—not Cloudflare—and you can architect around that."
