---

# 1. Cognee is the memory infrastructure

Cognee shouldn't be our intelligence.

It is the machinery that makes the company's world manageable.

Imagine a client uploads:

```text
47 sales calls
3 strategy decks
website
CRM export
customer research
competitor sites
campaign results
brand guidelines
```

Cognee helps us turn that mess into something queryable.

Instead of having:

```text
/document-018.pdf
/transcript-027.txt
/webpage-881.html
```

we eventually have concepts like:

```text
Audience:
Enterprise Operations Leader

Problem:
Implementation takes too long

Motivation:
Reduce organizational friction

Product:
Acme Platform

Claim:
Live in under 14 days

Evidence:
Customer interview #42
```

with relationships:

```text
Audience
   │
 experiences
   ▼
Problem

Product
   │
 solves
   ▼
Problem

Claim
   │
 supported_by
   ▼
Evidence
```

Cognee handles much of the difficult storage/search infrastructure underneath this.

But **we tell Cognee what those concepts are**.

---

# 2. We build the Brand Ontology

This is one of our core pieces.

It's our answer to:

> **What actually constitutes the world of a brand/company?**

For example:

```text
Company
Product
Audience
Persona
Problem
Need
Motivation
Objection
Trigger
Benefit
Feature
Proof
Claim
Competitor
Positioning
Narrative
Message
Offer
Campaign
Creative
Experiment
Metric
Decision
```

and relationships such as:

```text
Audience → experiences → Problem

Problem → driven_by → Motivation

Product → solves → Problem

Claim → supported_by → Proof

Positioning → targets → Audience

Positioning → differentiates_from → Competitor

Narrative → expresses → Positioning

Campaign → communicates → Message
```

Cognee provides graph machinery.

**We provide the marketing model of reality.**

That's proprietary.

---

# 3. We build the extraction intelligence

Cognee can parse/chunk/store.

But we should determine **what the system looks for**.

A sales call shouldn't be processed like a competitor website.

For a sales call, our algorithm might look for:

```text
Problems
Motivations
Desired outcomes
Objections
Buying triggers
Alternatives
Perceived value
Customer language
Emotional drivers
Evidence strength
```

For a competitor website:

```text
Positioning
Claims
Audience
Benefits
Narrative
Offers
Proof
Differentiators
Recent changes
```

For analytics:

```text
Observed behavior
Performance changes
Anomalies
Conversion patterns
Experiment outcomes
```

So we create intelligence modules such as:

```text
CustomerInterviewExtractor

CompetitorExtractor

PositioningExtractor

CampaignEvidenceExtractor

BrandBeliefExtractor
```

Those modules can call whatever LLM/model we choose through **our Model Router**.

Then they store structured results through Cognee.

---

# 4. We also decide what is actually true

This is another major proprietary component.

Suppose one founder interview says:

> Enterprise is our primary customer.

CRM data says:

> 72% of revenue is enterprise.

The website says:

> Built for companies of every size.

And another founder says:

> We're starting to move downmarket.

The system shouldn't collapse that into:

```text
ICP = enterprise
```

Instead:

```text
Observation A
source: founder
date: March
confidence: medium

Observation B
source: CRM
date: current
confidence: high

Observation C
source: website
status: public messaging

Observation D
source: founder
date: August
status: strategic intention
```

Our truth layer determines things like:

```text
OBSERVATION

HYPOTHESIS

PROPOSED FACT

CONFIRMED FACT

REJECTED

SUPERSEDED
```

with provenance, confidence and time.

Cognee can store all of that.

**We define what those states mean and how information moves between them.**

This could eventually become a major moat.

---

# 5. Graphiti handles “things change”

Graphiti is optional.

Its special purpose is:

> **Remember what was true when.**

For example:

```text
2025
ICP = startups

2026 Q1
ICP = mid-market

2026 Q3
ICP = enterprise
```

Instead of overwriting history, the box can understand evolution.

This matters for:

```text
positioning
competitors
strategy
customer preferences
campaigns
market conditions
product capabilities
```

Cognee already has some temporal functionality and Graphiti integration, so I wouldn't necessarily introduce Graphiti on day one.

Think:

> **Cognee = memory system.**
>
> **Graphiti = enhanced temporal memory.**

---

# 6. Our Box API hides all of this

Agents should never care whether we're using Cognee, Graphiti, Neo4j, Postgres or something else.

We give the rest of our system a tiny interface:

```text
Box.get(entity)

Box.search(query)

Box.related(entity)

Box.evidence(fact)

Box.history(entity)

Box.observe(...)

Box.propose(...)

Box.confirm(...)

Box.reject(...)

Box.recordDecision(...)
```

This is important.

Our code sees:

```text
Box
```

not:

```text
Cognee
```

So Cognee stays replaceable infrastructure.

---

# 7. Our Context Compiler is the bridge between memory and intelligence

The box may eventually contain millions of pieces of information.

An agent should not receive all of them.

Imagine the Strategist receives:

> Should we reposition around implementation speed?

The Context Compiler determines that it probably needs:

```text
current positioning

relevant ICP

customer complaints about implementation

purchase motivations

sales objections

competitor positioning

existing implementation claims

proof behind those claims

previous strategic decisions

relevant campaign results
```

It might compile 100 useful pieces of information from 100,000 available pieces.

Then:

```text
THE BOX
   ↓
Context Compiler
   ↓
compact ContextPackage
   ↓
Strategist
```

This is one of our most important algorithms.

Cognee tells us:

> what information exists.

Our compiler determines:

> **what information matters right now.**

---

# 8. LangGraph defines how each expert thinks

Once the Strategist gets the right context, another question begins:

> **What should it do with that information?**

That's where LangGraph becomes valuable.

We can encode:

```text
STRATEGIST

understand objective
       ↓
identify strategic tension
       ↓
generate competing hypotheses
       ↓
collect supporting evidence
       ↓
collect contradicting evidence
       ↓
evaluate differentiation
       ↓
evaluate customer relevance
       ↓
critic attack
       ↓
confidence sufficient?
      / \
    no   yes
    ↓     ↓
research decide
more
```

Researcher gets a completely different graph.

Brand Guardian gets another.

Storyteller another.

So these agents don't merely have different personalities.

They have different **cognitive architectures**.

This is another large part of our IP.

---

# 9. Our Model Router supplies the intelligence

Cognee, LangGraph, extraction algorithms and agents may all need LLMs.

I wouldn't let every framework independently decide which model to use.

We create:

```text
                 MODEL ROUTER

          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          ▼          ▼          ▼
       OpenAI     Anthropic   DeepSeek
          ▼          ▼          ▼
        local / other models etc.
```

Then our code can specify:

```text
cheap extraction
→ Model A

difficult strategy
→ Model B

classification
→ small fast model

creative exploration
→ Model C
```

This gives us control over:

```text
quality
cost
latency
fallbacks
privacy
```

Again, frameworks stay replaceable.

---

# 10. Harness makes those brains into persistent little guys

LangGraph says:

> how the Strategist thinks.

Harness says:

> **there is a Strategist.**

Harness handles things like:

```text
Strategist exists
Strategist has a session
Strategist has these tools
Strategist has these permissions
Strategist is currently working
Strategist needs approval
Strategist called HubSpot
Strategist's run failed
Strategist resumed
```

So the relationship is:

```text
HARNESS
"Who am I and what can I do?"

        ↓

LANGGRAPH
"How do I think?"

        ↓

BOX
"What do I know?"
```

That's the simplest mental model.

---

# 11. Harness also gives the agents hands

Through APIs/MCP/tools:

```text
Researcher
→ web search

Growth
→ analytics

Strategist
→ Brand Core

Campaign agent
→ HubSpot

Creative
→ image/video systems

Content agent
→ CMS
```

Harness can manage the execution and permission layer.

We shouldn't rebuild generic tool-calling infrastructure.

What we **do** build are domain-specific tools like:

```text
brand.find_customer_evidence()

brand.compare_positioning()

campaign.create_experiment()

brand.propose_decision()
```

Underneath those might simply call existing APIs.

---

# 12. Then we build the actual product

This is the part customers see.

Not LangGraph.

Not Cognee.

Not Harness.

The experience is:

```text
Researcher found something.

Strategist has an opinion.

Storyteller created something.

Brand Guardian objects.

Growth found a result.
```

And those become feed posts.

For example:

> 🔵 Researcher
> 14 of the last 23 customer calls mention implementation effort. This theme has increased over the past three months.

Then:

> 🟡 Strategist
> This may represent a positioning opportunity. Competitors emphasize capability, while customers increasingly care about implementation friction.

Then perhaps:

> 🟣 Storyteller
> I developed three narrative territories around “time to value.”

The infrastructure disappears.

---

# 13. The little guys visualize the actual system

The avatars aren't just decoration.

We can map real LangGraph/Harness states:

```text
Researcher

SEARCHING
→ scanning animation

COMPARING
→ objects move side by side

CONNECTING
→ particles connect

SYNTHESIZING
→ objects converge

UNCERTAIN
→ unstable motion

PRESENTING
→ settles with result
```

So the motion becomes a visual language for what the intelligence is actually doing.

---

# 14. The learning loop brings everything back

Eventually:

```text
agent produces recommendation
        ↓
human approves/rejects/comments
        ↓
action happens
        ↓
performance observed
        ↓
new evidence enters box
        ↓
beliefs/hypotheses updated
        ↓
future agents get better context
```

But crucially:

```text
👍 like
≠ truth
```

and:

```text
campaign worked
≠ automatically causal truth
```

We build the semantics for how feedback affects confidence, hypotheses, decisions and canonical knowledge.

That learning logic is another proprietary part.

---

# So what exactly are we building ourselves?

This is the important distinction.

| Layer | Existing infrastructure | We build |
|---|---|---|
| File parsing | Cognee/loaders | almost nothing |
| Chunk storage | Cognee | custom rules where useful |
| Vector storage | Cognee/provider | no |
| Graph infrastructure | Cognee | no |
| Temporal graph | Graphiti/Cognee | our semantics |
| Embeddings | existing models | routing/config |
| Model APIs | existing providers | Model Router |
| Agent runtime | Harness | thin adapter |
| Tool runtime | Harness/MCP | domain tools |
| Workflow engine | LangGraph | **graphs themselves** |
| Persistence | Cognee/Harness/LangGraph | boundaries/IDs |
| **Brand ontology** | — | **YES** |
| **Extraction intelligence** | generic primitives | **YES** |
| **Truth model** | storage primitives | **YES** |
| **Contradiction logic** | — | **YES** |
| **Context Compiler** | retrieval primitives | **YES** |
| **Marketing reasoning** | LangGraph primitives | **YES** |
| **Learning algorithms** | — | **YES** |
| **Evaluations** | libraries may help | **YES** |
| **Feed semantics** | — | **YES** |
| **Product UI** | React/etc. | **YES** |
| **Avatar system** | animation libs | **YES** |
| **Client configuration** | — | **YES** |

And that's exactly where I want the project to land.

# A complete example

Suppose tomorrow a new customer interview arrives.

### Step 1 — ingestion

```text
Zoom transcript
     ↓
Cognee loader
```

### Step 2 — our extraction

Our Customer Intelligence Extractor finds:

```text
Problem:
"Setup requires too much internal coordination"

Motivation:
"Get value without involving five departments"

Objection:
"Implementation risk"

Quote:
"We just don't have time for another six-month rollout."
```

### Step 3 — store it

Cognee stores the source, entities, relationships, embeddings and provenance.

Our truth system labels them initially as:

```text
observations
```

not facts.

### Step 4 — pattern emerges

The system notices 17 similar observations.

Our intelligence layer proposes:

```text
Hypothesis:

Implementation friction is becoming
a major purchase criterion for enterprise buyers.

confidence: 0.78
```

### Step 5 — feed

Researcher posts:

> I'm seeing a growing implementation-friction pattern across enterprise interviews.

### Step 6 — Strategist is triggered

Context Compiler gathers:

```text
17 interview observations
current positioning
competitor positioning
sales objections
product implementation metrics
existing proof
historical positioning decisions
```

### Step 7 — LangGraph thinks

Strategist:

```text
hypothesize
→ challenge
→ compare competitors
→ inspect customer evidence
→ check proof
→ evaluate alternatives
→ recommend
```

### Step 8 — Harness manages it

Harness handles:

```text
agent session
tools
model calls
permissions
runtime
events
```

### Step 9 — recommendation

Feed:

> 🟡 Strategist
> We have enough evidence to test implementation speed as a secondary positioning pillar. I would not make it the primary positioning yet.

Human:

**Approve experiment**

### Step 10 — action

Growth agent creates an experiment.

### Step 11 — learning

Results return to the box.

Now the company has learned something.

That's essentially the entire product.

# And therefore the project is much smaller than it initially sounds

At first, “AI Marketing Operating System with a company world model and persistent specialist agents” sounds like we need to invent:

```text
database architecture
knowledge graph
vector DB
document parsing
agent framework
tool framework
workflow engine
memory system
MCP
LLM abstraction
etc.
```

We don't.

We can reuse most of that.

What we're really building is:

> **A formal model of marketing reality.**
>
> **Algorithms that turn messy evidence into that model.**
>
> **Algorithms that select the right context.**
>
> **Expert cognitive architectures that reason over it.**
>
> **A learning system that improves the model over time.**
>
> **A beautiful human interface for interacting with that intelligence.**

That is still ambitious.

But it's a much better kind of ambitious.

We're spending engineering effort on **how an exceptional marketer understands a company and makes decisions**, rather than on implementing another vector database wrapper or agent loop.

And I think that's the correct architectural north star for the complete project. memcite

## Assistant

Yes — and this is actually a **very good fit for the architecture we want**.

But with one nuance:

> Cognee gives us the primitives for progressive disclosure, but **we should define the actual abstraction hierarchy ourselves**.

Cognee already supports raw chunks, pre-generated **hierarchical summaries**, graph entities/relationships, dataset-level/topic indexes, semantic indexes, NodeSets, and custom DataPoint types. Retrieval can also be restricted by dataset, node type, NodeSet, search strategy, and `top_k`. citeturn476131search10turn476131search0turn212048search14

So we could build our box like this:

```text
LEVEL 5 — COMPANY MODEL
────────────────────────
"Acme wins by..."
"Primary strategic tension..."
"Current market position..."

            ↓ drill down

LEVEL 4 — STRATEGIC KNOWLEDGE
─────────────────────────────
Positioning
ICP
Narratives
Brand principles
Key customer motivations
Strategic decisions

            ↓

LEVEL 3 — SYNTHESIZED INSIGHTS
──────────────────────────────
"Implementation friction is a
major enterprise buying concern"

"Three customer segments repeatedly
mention lack of internal resources"

            ↓

LEVEL 2 — OBSERVATIONS / FACTS
──────────────────────────────
Customer pain
Objection
Claim
Competitor message
CRM pattern
Campaign result

            ↓

LEVEL 1 — EVIDENCE
──────────────────
Customer quotes
Website sections
Analytics records
CRM records
Sales-call moments

            ↓

LEVEL 0 — RAW SOURCE
────────────────────
PDF
Call transcript
CRM object
Webpage
Analytics event
```

That is essentially **progressive disclosure for knowledge**.

The Strategist doesn't initially receive 300 customer-call chunks.

It might initially see:

> “Implementation friction is a high-confidence enterprise pain.”

If it needs to challenge that conclusion:

```text
Insight
   ↓
supporting observations
   ↓
customer quotes
   ↓
original transcripts
```

So the agent can progressively **zoom into the evidence**.

### Cognee already has pieces of this

Its standard Cognify pipeline itself creates several representations:

```text
Document
   ↓
Chunks
   ↓
Entities + relationships
   ↓
Summaries
   ↓
Vector indexes + graph
```

and the summaries are separately indexed for retrieval. citeturn476131search5turn476131search8

More recently, Cognee also added an optional **Topic Index** that groups documents into topic clusters and produces short dataset-level overviews, specifically to improve broader/high-level retrieval. citeturn476131search1

So it already naturally moves toward:

```text
raw
↓
granular
↓
structured
↓
summarized
↓
overview
```

---

## But I wouldn't use Cognee's hierarchy blindly

I'd create **our own semantic abstraction levels**.

For example, our custom objects could be:

```text
Source
↓
Evidence
↓
Observation
↓
Pattern
↓
Insight
↓
Hypothesis
↓
ConfirmedKnowledge
↓
StrategicPrinciple
```

Each one can be its own Cognee `DataPoint` type.

Then relationships preserve the chain:

```text
StrategicPrinciple

"Speed-to-value is central
to enterprise positioning"

        │ derived_from
        ▼

ConfirmedInsight

"Implementation speed strongly
influences enterprise purchases"

        │ supported_by
        ▼

Pattern

18/24 interviews mention
implementation friction

        │ evidenced_by
        ▼

Observations

        │ source
        ▼

Actual customer quotes
```

This is **much better than repeatedly summarizing summaries**, because we preserve provenance.

---

# Then retrieval becomes progressive too

Our Context Compiler could start cheaply at a high level.

For example:

```text
Question:

"Should we change our
enterprise positioning?"

        ↓

Search L4/L5 first

Positioning
Strategic decisions
ICP
Current major insights
```

Maybe that's enough.

If not:

```text
↓ expand

L3 insights
competitor patterns
customer themes
```

Still uncertain?

```text
↓ expand

L2 observations
```

Need verification?

```text
↓ expand

L1 evidence
customer quotes
CRM records
```

Only rarely:

```text
↓ expand

L0 original documents
```

That's exactly what I'd want.

It saves tokens and probably improves reasoning because the model isn't initially buried under irrelevant detail.

---

## Cognee lets us implement this pretty elegantly

Search can target different representations directly. Cognee exposes retrieval modes for `SUMMARIES`, raw `CHUNKS`, graph relationships, temporal data and graph+summary combinations. It also supports filtering by custom DataPoint type. citeturn212048search0turn212048search5

And if those aren't enough, its retriever system is pluggable: you can register a custom retriever implementing Cognee's retrieval interface. citeturn212048search1

So we could eventually create:

```text
BrandProgressiveRetriever
```

whose behavior is literally:

```text
1. search strategic abstractions
2. evaluate sufficiency/confidence
3. expand into insights if necessary
4. expand into evidence if necessary
5. return provenance chain
```

That would fit underneath our Context Compiler beautifully.

---

# I would actually make this a central principle of the box

Not:

```text
Agent → search all company knowledge
```

but:

```text
             THE BOX

       abstract / compressed
               ▲
               │
          Strategic model
               │
             Insights
               │
             Patterns
               │
          Observations
               │
            Evidence
               │
          Raw sources
               ▼

       concrete / detailed
```

Then agents can move **up and down the abstraction ladder**.

A Storyteller might mostly operate near:

```text
Strategic model
Narratives
Insights
```

Researcher might regularly descend into:

```text
Observations
Evidence
Raw sources
```

Brand Guardian might do:

```text
Claim
 ↓
Evidence
 ↓
Original source
```

Strategist might oscillate:

```text
Strategic model
 ↕
Insights
 ↕
Evidence
```

That's an excellent match for specialized agents.

### And it makes the Context Compiler much smarter

Instead of just asking:

> “Which documents are similar to this query?”

it asks two things:

> **What knowledge is relevant?**

and

> **At what level of abstraction should I provide it?**

That second question is potentially very important.

So yes: **Cognee can support this architecture quite well**, including existing hierarchical summaries and topic indexes, while letting us create our own richer abstraction layers through custom DataPoints, pipelines and retrievers. citeturn476131search11turn476131search6

And I would absolutely build the box this way rather than having one flat graph/vector index. It could make the whole agent system both cheaper and substantially more intelligent. memcite

## Assistant

Yes. I researched the remaining gaps against the architecture we’ve been building, and there are **a few more pieces I would reuse rather than build**.

The biggest finding is that we are missing one important layer in our current picture: **the box should probably have two kinds of memory, not one**.

Cognee is excellent for *semantic company knowledge*—brand facts, customer insights, evidence, relationships, positioning, narratives, documents. But campaign spend, conversion rates, CRM tables, daily traffic, funnel events, cohort data, etc. are fundamentally **analytical data**, and we should not force all of that into a knowledge graph.

With that correction, I think we can get quite close to a system where most of our engineering is indeed concentrated on intelligence.

## 1. Nango could remove most of our integration work

This one is a **very strong fit**.

Eventually every client will say:

> Connect our HubSpot.

> Connect Google Analytics.

> Connect Meta.

> Connect Notion.

> Connect Slack.

> Connect our CRM.

The annoying part isn't usually calling an API. It's OAuth, token refresh, credential storage, rate limits, pagination, syncing, retries, webhooks, tenant isolation and keeping everything working when providers change.

Nango is explicitly built to handle that integration layer. Its current docs say it supports 700+ APIs and handles authentication, credential management, execution, retries, rate limits, observability, environments and tenant isolation. It can expose integration functions through APIs, SDKs or MCP, and supports keeping external data synchronized. citeturn975422search6turn975422search1

So instead of:

```text
OUR CODE

HubSpot OAuth
HubSpot refresh tokens
HubSpot pagination
HubSpot sync logic

Slack OAuth
Slack refresh
Slack sync

Google OAuth
Google refresh
Google sync

Meta auth
Meta token handling
...
```

we get:

```text
             NANGO

HubSpot ──────┐
Slack ────────┤
Google ───────┼──→ our normalized adapters
Meta ─────────┤
Notion ───────┤
etc. ─────────┘
```

Then **we only write the interesting mapping**:

```text
HubSpotContact
      ↓
our interpretation
      ↓
Customer / Audience / Revenue signal
```

Nango also handles both directions, which is valuable because later Harness agents can use the same integration infrastructure to **act** rather than merely ingest data. citeturn565791search8turn565791search0

So I would probably add Nango.

---

## 2. LiteLLM should probably become our Model Router

We've kept talking about building a `ModelRouter`.

I don't think we need to build most of it.

LiteLLM already provides a central OpenAI-compatible gateway across 100+ model providers, with provider normalization, retries, fallbacks, routing, cost tracking, budgets, authentication and rate limiting. citeturn121825search6

So:

```text
                 OUR SYSTEM
                     │
                     ▼
                  LiteLLM
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐
       ▼             ▼              ▼
     OpenAI       Anthropic      DeepSeek
       │             │              │
     Gemini       Mistral         local
```

Our code only says:

```text
model_role = "cheap_extraction"
```

or:

```text
model_role = "deep_strategy"
```

and our small configuration maps that to actual models.

For example:

```text
customer_extraction
→ cheap structured-output model

strategic synthesis
→ strongest reasoning model

creative exploration
→ creative model

classification
→ tiny fast model
```

LiteLLM handles much of the provider plumbing underneath. citeturn121825search6

This is another piece I would **not build ourselves**.

---

## 3. Langfuse could become our AI laboratory

This one is potentially extremely important.

If we are going to spend most of our time developing intelligence algorithms, we need to answer:

> Did Strategist v17 actually become better than Strategist v16?

> Did the new Context Compiler improve results?

> Is CustomerExtractor v8 missing fewer motivations?

> Which model gives us the best quality/cost ratio?

> Why did this particular agent make a bad recommendation?

Building that evaluation infrastructure ourselves would be a mistake.

Langfuse is an open-source/self-hostable AI engineering platform combining tracing, prompt management, datasets, experiments, human feedback and automated evaluations. Its LangGraph integration can automatically trace graph execution, nested agents and scores, while its OpenTelemetry foundation lets us instrument custom systems too. citeturn121825search1turn297390search1turn297390search8

Imagine:

```text
Strategist v12
────────────────

Strategic relevance     8.4
Evidence grounding      9.1
Differentiation         6.8
Brand coherence         9.0
Cost                    €0.19
Latency                 12.4 sec

Strategist v13
────────────────

Strategic relevance     9.0 ↑
Evidence grounding      9.2 ↑
Differentiation         8.1 ↑
Brand coherence         8.9
Cost                    €0.17 ↓
Latency                 10.2 sec ↓
```

That's the development environment we want.

Langfuse supports deterministic code evaluators, model judges, datasets, experiments, manual annotation and production feedback. citeturn121825search10turn121825search12

So I'd treat:

> **Langfuse = laboratory for our intelligence.**

Very strong addition.

## 4. DuckDB fills a missing part of the box

This is the architectural correction I mentioned.

Suppose Growth asks:

> Which audience had the highest CAC-adjusted LTV during the last six months?

That's not really a Cognee knowledge-graph problem.

It's SQL.

Similarly:

```text
Ad spend
Conversions
Revenue
CTR
CAC
LTV
Traffic
Cohorts
Funnel stages
Experiment results
CRM records
```

should remain structured/numeric.

I'd therefore give the Box a small **analytics plane**.

DuckDB is attractive because it can directly query things like Parquet files, object storage and Postgres rather than forcing us to build a large warehouse immediately. Its Postgres extension can query attached PostgreSQL databases directly, and it can query Parquet stored in S3-compatible storage. citeturn734296search2turn734296search11

So:

```text
             THE BOX

     ┌─────────┴─────────┐
     ▼                   ▼

 KNOWLEDGE            ANALYTICS
  Cognee               DuckDB

 "Customers care      CAC = €432
  about speed"        CVR = 4.7%

 Positioning          revenue
 Evidence             funnel
 Narratives           cohorts
 Quotes               experiments
 Competitors          metrics
```

And the Context Compiler can combine them.

For example:

```text
Strategist asks:

"Is implementation speed
a meaningful positioning opportunity?"

             ↓

Knowledge side:
18 customer interviews mention it

             +

Analytics side:
campaigns emphasizing speed
converted 31% better

             +

Brand side:
we actually have proof for
14-day implementation

             ↓

Context Compiler
```

That's dramatically better than trying to stuff everything into one graph.

At very high scale we could later replace/augment DuckDB with something like ClickHouse, which is specifically designed for high-volume analytical workloads. citeturn734296search7

But I would **not start with ClickHouse**.

# Then there are two tools that could improve our intelligence itself

These are more interesting than infrastructure.

## DSPy could help us optimize the algorithms

This might eventually be one of the most valuable additions.

DSPy lets you define LLM operations as typed input/output programs and then **optimize them against an evaluation metric and training examples**, rather than manually tweaking prompts forever. citeturn382325search0

Imagine our customer extractor:

```text
INPUT

sales-call segment

      ↓

CustomerInsightExtractor

      ↓

OUTPUT

problem
motivation
objection
trigger
desired_outcome
evidence
confidence
```

Initially we write it.

Then we collect 500 examples where we've manually judged what the correct extraction should have been.

DSPy can optimize the LLM program against our score.

Conceptually:

```text
our extractor
     ↓
500 examples
     ↓
our quality metric
     ↓
DSPy optimizer
     ↓
better extractor
```

DSPy's current optimization model explicitly works this way: define a program, examples and a scoring metric, then compile/optimize the program. citeturn382325search0

This could apply to:

```text
CustomerInsightExtractor
CompetitorExtractor
ContextQueryGenerator
HypothesisGenerator
EvidenceEvaluator
StrategicCritic
NarrativeEvaluator
```

So LangGraph and DSPy have different roles:

```text
LANGGRAPH

defines:
HOW THE THINKING PROCESS FLOWS

DSPy

optimizes:
HOW WELL INDIVIDUAL THINKING OPERATIONS WORK
```

That's potentially powerful.

I would introduce DSPy **after we have evaluation datasets**, not before.

---

# Ragas could specifically help us improve the Context Compiler

Langfuse gives us the general evaluation environment.

Ragas gives us useful retrieval-specific metrics.

For example, **context precision** measures whether relevant information is ranked ahead of irrelevant information, while **context recall** measures whether our retrieval failed to include important evidence. Ragas also includes metrics for things like noise sensitivity, faithfulness and agent/tool behavior. citeturn174243search0turn174243search2turn174243search3

That maps almost perfectly to our Context Compiler.

We could test:

```text
Question:

"Should Acme emphasize speed
in enterprise positioning?"
```

Human expert says the ideal context contains:

```text
A
B
C
D
E
```

Compiler v1 returns:

```text
A
B
D
X
Y
```

Compiler v2 returns:

```text
A
B
C
D
E
```

Now we can objectively improve retrieval rather than saying:

> “v2 feels smarter.”

Ragas already documents integration with Langfuse, so scores can be attached to the traces we're already collecting. citeturn174243search1

That combination is very attractive:

```text
Context Compiler
      ↓
Ragas evaluates retrieval
      ↓
Langfuse stores experiments
      ↓
DSPy/our algorithms improve it
```

This creates an actual **intelligence-development loop**.

---

# Background processing is another thing we shouldn't build

Eventually there will be lots of:

```text
sync CRM every hour

reprocess 3,000 interviews

update competitor research

generate nightly summaries

rebuild abstraction indexes

run evaluation suite

process uploaded documents
```

Those jobs need queues, retries, durability, concurrency limits, scheduling and progress reporting.

Trigger.dev already provides durable TypeScript background tasks, retries, queues, schedules and real-time frontend status updates, and can be cloud-hosted or self-hosted. citeturn121825search2turn121825search15turn121825search14

But I would not add it immediately.

Harness already handles agent work.

Nango handles integration sync work.

If we start accumulating lots of **non-agent application jobs**, then add Trigger.

So:

```text
Harness
= agents working

Nango
= external integrations syncing

Trigger
= miscellaneous durable backend jobs
```

No overlap if we keep those boundaries.

---

# Two things I'd postpone

**OpenFGA** is interesting if our permissions become complex—e.g. one agency employee can see Brand A but not Brand B, freelancers can access campaigns but not customer evidence, clients can share selected objects, and agents have their own resource permissions. OpenFGA provides relationship-based authorization around users, objects and relations. citeturn565791search13turn565791search12

But for an early managed product, standard tenant roles plus Cognee dataset isolation and Harness tool scopes should probably suffice.

Similarly, **Infisical** is a strong secrets-management option for API keys, database credentials and machine identities, with centralized versioned secrets and fine-grained access control. citeturn307454search1turn307454search7

But Nango already handles customer OAuth credentials, so I wouldn't add Infisical until our own infrastructure secrets become complicated.

---

# And I would use PostHog for our product, not the box

We'll want to know:

> Do clients actually read Researcher posts?

> What percentage of recommendations get approved?

> Which agents get chatted with?

> Do users drill from insight → evidence?

> Does the avatar activity help or distract?

PostHog currently combines product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, surveys and related product-development tooling. citeturn112775search3

That's useful for improving **our UI/product**.

I wouldn't make PostHog part of the core Brand Box.

## Assistant

That makes sense. **DSPy is not useful yet if you don’t have a dataset and a reliable way to score “better.”**

Right now, you’re better off explicitly designing the reasoning yourself.

So the flow becomes:

```text
Brand Core
   ↓
Context Compiler
   ↓
Your reasoning logic
   ↓
LangGraph executes it
   ↓
Harness runs the agent around it
   ↓
Feed / action
```

Your main job is to encode things like:

```text
Strategist:
- identify the strategic tension
- generate competing hypotheses
- look for supporting evidence
- look for disconfirming evidence
- compare alternatives
- score tradeoffs
- escalate when confidence is low
- produce a recommendation
```

That logic can be very explicit. You can define thresholds, branches, critic passes, required evidence, stopping conditions, and when another agent should be consulted.

And at this stage, that is actually useful research in itself: you’re discovering **what a good marketing reasoning process should be**.

Later, naturally, you’ll accumulate data from real usage:

```text
task
→ context provided
→ reasoning path
→ recommendation
→ founder feedback
→ approval/rejection
→ eventual outcome
```

Then you might eventually have hundreds or thousands of examples of:

> what context worked, what reasoning pattern worked, and which outputs humans considered strong.

At that point tools like DSPy become more interesting, because you can say:

> “Here are 800 real strategy cases and our quality metric. Improve this module.”

But before then, automatic optimization could easily optimize against a weak or artificial metric.

So I would actually remove DSPy from the initial architecture entirely.

The leaner stack becomes:

```text
COGNEE
knowledge infrastructure

DUCKDB
analytics

NANGO
external integrations

LITELLM
model routing

LANGGRAPH
our reasoning algorithms

DEEPSEEK HARNESS
agent runtime

LANGFUSE
tracing + evaluation + future dataset

OUR PRODUCT
ontology
extraction logic
truth system
context compiler
reasoning logic
feed + avatars
```

**Langfuse is still worth keeping**, even without training data, because from day one it can record the cases that may eventually *become* your evaluation/training dataset.

So rather than trying to optimize the intelligence automatically now:

> **design it manually → observe it → correct it → collect examples → formalize evaluation → optimize later.**

That is a much more sensible progression for where the product is today. memcite

### What Harness already gives us

DeepSeek Harness now has quite substantial subagent infrastructure. An agent can delegate work to child agents; those children can be durable/continuable, receive follow-up work, be interrupted, report back to their parent, and be discovered/listed. It even has optional model-facing controls such as `send_message`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents`. fileciteturn27file0

So Harness can already handle things like:

```text
Strategist
    ↓ delegates
Researcher

Researcher works
    ↓
reports result

Strategist receives report
    ↓
continues
```

It also owns the actual agent sessions, inboxes, cancellation, lifecycle and persistent child sessions. fileciteturn27file0

We absolutely should reuse that rather than building an agent messaging runtime.

### LangGraph covers coordination inside a reasoning process

LangGraph gives us shared state, subgraphs, branching and explicit handoffs. Its multi-agent architecture lets one agent/subgraph pass controlled state to another, and it explicitly emphasizes that **we decide exactly what context crosses between agents** rather than blindly sending all conversation history. citeturn587325search0turn587325search1

So if Strategist's reasoning algorithm says:

```text
generate hypothesis
       ↓
need customer evidence?
       ↓ yes
call Researcher
       ↓
ResearcherGraph
       ↓
return EvidencePackage
       ↓
continue strategy process
```

LangGraph already handles that structure. citeturn587325search3turn587325search4

---

# What is actually missing

We need a **Work Coordination Layer** specific to our product.

Not a huge system. Think of it as the company's internal AI task board.

Instead of:

> “Hey Researcher, can you look into competitors and tell me what you think?”

Strategist creates something structured:

```text
Task

type:
COMPETITOR_RESEARCH

objective:
Determine whether competitors emphasize
implementation speed.

requested_by:
Strategist

assigned_to:
Researcher

context:
[references into Brand Box]

required_output:
CompetitorEvidencePackage

priority:
high

status:
assigned
```

Researcher eventually returns:

```text
WorkResult

task_id:
123

findings:
[...]

evidence:
[...]

confidence:
0.87

unresolved_questions:
[...]

box_references:
[...]
```

That's the piece I think **we should build**.

And it should be small.

---

# I would create three primitives

### `Task`

Something an agent wants done.

```text
Task
├── id
├── type
├── objective
├── requested_by
├── assigned_to
├── context_refs
├── dependencies
├── expected_output_schema
├── priority
└── status
```

### `Artifact / Result`

Something an agent produced.

```text
Result
├── task_id
├── producer
├── structured_output
├── evidence_refs
├── confidence
├── assumptions
└── created_at
```

### `Event`

Something that happened.

```text
TaskCreated
TaskAssigned
TaskStarted
ResearchStarted
EvidenceFound
HypothesisCreated
ReviewRequested
TaskCompleted
DecisionApproved
DecisionRejected
```

That's enough to power a surprisingly large amount of the system.

---

# Then communication becomes elegant

Imagine Researcher discovers something that matters to Strategist.

We **don't** need:

```text
Researcher → random message → Strategist
```

Instead:

```text
Researcher
     ↓
creates Insight

"Competitors have shifted toward
implementation simplicity."

     ↓
stored in Box

     +
emits InsightCreated

     ↓
Director / Strategist sees event
```

Now the information isn't trapped inside an agent conversation.

It's part of the company's knowledge.

That's much stronger.

---

# This is especially important for our Box

The Box should function as the **shared world agents coordinate through**.

For example:

```text
             BRAND BOX

       Customer Insight
             │
             │ referenced by
             ▼
Researcher ────── Strategist
                    │
                    │ creates
                    ▼
              Positioning Hypothesis
                    │
                    ▼
               Storyteller
                    │
                    ▼
                 Narrative
```

Agents aren't sending huge amounts of knowledge to each other.

They're saying:

> “Look at Insight `#1842`.”

The actual information remains in the Box.

That keeps context compact and gives us provenance.

---

# The Director becomes a manager, not a super-brain

I'd give one agent/system role responsibility for coordination:

```text
                  DIRECTOR

                     │

       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ▼             ▼             ▼
 Researcher      Strategist     Growth
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     ▼
                  The Box
```

The Director's job isn't to redo everyone's reasoning.

It handles things like:

> Who should work on this?

> Can these tasks run in parallel?

> Does Strategist need Researcher's result first?

> Does Brand Guardian need to review this?

> Does this need human approval?

> Is work duplicated?

> Has something stalled?

Then specialist agents do the actual intellectual work.

---

# An example

User says:

> “I think we need a new positioning direction.”

Director turns that into:

```text
PROJECT
New positioning exploration
```

and creates:

```text
Task A
Research customer perception
→ Researcher

Task B
Analyze competitor positions
→ Researcher

Task C
Analyze historical campaign performance
→ Growth
```

A and B could run in parallel.

Growth queries analytics.

Results become structured artifacts:

```text
CustomerEvidencePackage

CompetitiveLandscape

PerformanceEvidence
```

Then:

```text
A ──┐
B ──┼──→ Strategy Task
C ──┘
```

Strategist's LangGraph runs its reasoning process.

It outputs:

```text
PositioningRecommendation
```

Then:

```text
PositioningRecommendation
        ↓
Brand Guardian
        ↓
review
        ↓
Human approval
```

And every step creates feed events.

---

# This also solves our avatar states naturally

The work system knows:

```text
Researcher
task = competitor research
status = working
phase = searching
```

Therefore UI:

```text
🔵 Researcher
SCANNING
```

Later LangGraph enters evidence comparison:

```text
phase = comparing
```

Avatar changes.

Then:

```text
TaskCompleted
```

Researcher settles and publishes a feed post.

So the work-management system becomes part of the bridge between **backend reality and little-guy animation**.

---

# Do we need Kafka, Temporal, CrewAI, AutoGen, another multi-agent framework, etc.?

**No, not initially.**

That would probably make the system worse.

We already have:

```text
Harness
→ agent lifecycle + delegation + messaging

LangGraph
→ cognitive/workflow coordination

Postgres
→ durable product/work state

Cognee
→ shared company knowledge

Trigger.dev later
→ generic long-running backend jobs
```

LangGraph itself is already meant for durable stateful workflows and multi-agent orchestration. citeturn587325search1turn587325search6

Adding yet another “multi-agent management framework” would mostly duplicate responsibilities.

---

# The architecture I'd use

```text
                    USER
                      │
                      ▼
                  DIRECTOR
                      │
             creates structured
                    TASKS
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼             ▼             ▼
   Researcher     Strategist      Growth
   HARNESS        HARNESS         HARNESS
        │             │             │
   LangGraph      LangGraph      LangGraph
   cognition      cognition      cognition
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      │
                  WORK LEDGER
                [our Postgres]
                      │
              tasks / results
              dependencies
              statuses/events
                      │
        ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
        ▼                           ▼
      BOX                         FEED
    Cognee                     Product UI
      │                           │
 shared knowledge             little guys
```

The **Work Ledger** is the small missing piece.

---

## And I think we should own it

Because the semantics are product-specific.

A generic framework knows:

> agent A sent message B.

We care about:

> Researcher produced evidence that supports Hypothesis X, Strategist used it in Decision Y, Brand Guardian challenged Claim Z, founder approved the resulting experiment.

Those are **marketing work semantics**.

I'd probably make our central domain objects something like:

```text
Task
Artifact
Observation
Insight
Hypothesis
Recommendation
Decision
Experiment
Result
Event
```

Then agents create and transform these objects.

That's much more powerful than creating a Slack clone for AI agents.

So the answer is:

> **Yes, we need intra-agent work coordination.**
>
> **No, we probably don't need another infrastructure product for it.**
>
> Harness + LangGraph give us most of the generic machinery; we should build a **thin structured Work Ledger + event protocol** that expresses how our particular AI marketing team works.

And I think that layer, together with the Box, is what turns a collection of agents into an actual **AI organization**. memcite

## User

would we need mem0?

## Assistant

Probably **not**—at least not in the architecture we’re converging on.

Mem0 is primarily a **persistent personalization/conversational-memory layer for agents**. It stores things like user preferences, session memories, agent memories, and organizational memories, and can automatically extract/retrieve useful memories from conversations. It also has optional graph memory for relationship-aware recall. citeturn559137search0turn559137search5

The problem is that we already have those responsibilities covered.

```text
HARNESS
= agent session / conversation / runtime history

COGNEE
= company knowledge / long-term organizational memory
= graph / evidence / semantic retrieval
= even short-term session memory if we want it

OUR POSTGRES
= tasks / work / approvals / decisions

OUR CONTEXT COMPILER
= decides what memory enters an agent's context
```

Cognee now explicitly has session memory too: a `(user_id, session_id)` scope can hold short-term conversation information, while permanent knowledge lives in its graph-backed memory. citeturn944400search8turn944400search9

So adding Mem0 would give us something like:

```text
Harness memory
     +
Cognee memory
     +
Mem0 memory
```

and then we'd have to answer:

> Which system owns this fact?

> Where does the founder's preference live?

> Where does an agent remember something it learned yesterday?

> Which system should the Context Compiler query?

> What happens if Mem0 remembers something that contradicts the Brand Box?

That's unnecessary complexity.

### There is one area where Mem0 could eventually be useful

Suppose users interact heavily with the little guys and we want very personalized behavior:

```text
Founder Sarah
→ hates long recommendations
→ prefers evidence before creative ideas
→ usually wants 3 alternatives
→ doesn't want Growth to change spend without asking
→ repeatedly rejects aggressive messaging
```

Mem0 is specifically designed for this kind of **automatic conversational personalization across sessions**. citeturn559137search3turn559137search14

Then we *could* use:

```text
Mem0
= memory about the HUMAN

Cognee
= memory about the COMPANY
```

That is the only separation where I think it becomes architecturally clean.

For example:

```text
              SARAH
                │
              Mem0
        preferences/history
                │
                ▼
             AGENT

                ▲
                │
             Cognee
      company/brand knowledge
                │
             THE BOX
```

But even there, I wouldn't introduce it yet. A simple `UserProfile` object in our own database or Cognee would probably handle V1 perfectly well.

There is also a philosophical reason I'd keep Mem0 away from the Brand Box: Mem0 is intentionally designed to **automatically decide useful things to remember from interactions**. Its current memory algorithm extracts and accumulates facts and performs entity linking and retrieval optimization. citeturn559137search0

Our Brand Box is deliberately stricter:

```text
conversation
    ↓
observation
    ↓
hypothesis
    ↓
evidence
    ↓
approval
    ↓
canonical truth
```

I don't want another generic memory engine independently deciding what becomes organizational truth.

So my current architecture would be:

```text
                   MEMORY

      ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
      │                             │

   HARNESS                       COGNEE
agent/session                  company world
runtime memory                organizational memory

      │                             │
      └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                     ▼
              Context Compiler
                     ▼
                  Agents
```

**No Mem0.**

Later, if we discover that *human-specific conversational personalization* is becoming a substantial engineering problem, Mem0 is worth reconsidering as a narrowly scoped **user-memory service**.

But right now it would mostly duplicate Cognee + Harness and make the memory architecture less clear rather than better. memcite

## User

arent there other systems already build for agent2agent communication and work that we could use to enhance our product? or does that add nore work than it solves instead if just creating our own light system

---

## Assistant

Yes. After looking at the current ecosystem, there **are** systems we can reuse—but I would only add one of them to our architecture now.

The important distinction is between:

> **using a standard protocol**, which can simplify us,

and

> **adding another multi-agent framework**, which would mostly duplicate things we already have.

The one I think we should seriously adopt is **A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol)**.

### A2A is almost exactly the standard vocabulary we were about to invent

A2A is now a Linux Foundation open standard for communication between independent agents. Its core concepts are already:

- `AgentCard` — what an agent is capable of
- `Task` — a stateful piece of work
- `Message` — communication
- `Artifact` — something produced by work
- `contextId` — grouping related work
- task states such as working, input-required, completed, failed, rejected, canceled

It supports structured data, files, streaming and long-running tasks. citeturn841607search0turn841607search3

That's remarkably close to what we were designing:

```text
OUR IDEA               A2A

Agent definition   →   AgentCard

Work Task          →   Task

Agent communication →  Message

Work Result        →   Artifact

Project/context    →   contextId

TaskCompleted      →   Task status/update
```

So rather than inventing all of the generic language ourselves, I would **design our Work Layer so it maps cleanly onto A2A**.

But there's an important twist.

## I would NOT make the internal little guys communicate over A2A

The A2A project itself explicitly says A2A is **not intended to define communication between an agent and its own subagents**. It is primarily a protocol between independent/opaque agent systems. For internal subagents, it recommends using the native framework mechanism. citeturn841607search1

That means our internal architecture should remain:

```text
            OUR AI ORGANIZATION

                 Director
                    │
          structured Task
                    │
          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
          ▼         ▼         ▼
      Researcher Strategist Growth
          │         │         │
          └──── Harness ──────┘
                messaging
                lifecycle
                reports
                subagents
```

Harness already supports continuable child agents, follow-up messages, reporting to parents, interruption, discovery/listing and durable child sessions. fileciteturn27file0

So using A2A **inside** that would be redundant.

Instead:

```text
INTERNAL
─────────────────────────

Harness native communication

EXTERNAL BOUNDARY
─────────────────────────

A2A
```

That is much cleaner.

---

## Where A2A becomes very valuable for our product

Imagine three years from now.

The client's company already has:

```text
Salesforce Agent
SAP Agent
internal Finance Agent
customer-service agent
our Marketing OS
```

Rather than building custom integrations between every AI system:

```text
                    A2A

Finance Agent ───────────────┐
                             │
Salesforce Agent ────────────┼── Our Marketing OS
                             │
SAP Agent ───────────────────┤
                             │
External research agent ─────┘
```

Each remains its own opaque system.

They can discover capabilities, issue tasks and return artifacts through a common protocol. That's exactly the use case A2A targets. citeturn472000search1turn841607search2

And this ecosystem has become fairly credible: A2A was originally created by Google, then donated to the Linux Foundation, with governance involving companies including AWS, Cisco, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow. citeturn841607search1

So future-proofing our work model around it makes sense.

---

# LangGraph also makes this easy later

Another positive finding: **LangGraph Agent Server already exposes A2A endpoints**.

A deployed LangGraph assistant can expose an A2A Agent Card and support A2A methods such as sending messages, streaming results and fetching task status. citeturn433337search0turn433337search1

So potentially:

```text
External Agent
      │
     A2A
      │
      ▼
Our LangGraph specialist
      │
      ▼
Harness / Box / reasoning
```

with relatively little adapter code.

That's exactly the sort of reuse we want.

---

# What about AGNTCY?

This is the more ambitious version.

AGNTCY is an open-source stack focused on an **Internet of Agents**. It has infrastructure for:

agent discovery, capability directories, decentralized identity, secure communication and multi-agent observability. citeturn528610search10

One interesting component is **SLIM**, a secure low-latency messaging layer for agents.

Think:

```text
A2A
= WHAT agents say

SLIM
= HOW those messages travel securely
```

SLIM provides things like secure messaging, group channels, RPC, reliable delivery, encryption and distributed routing. citeturn433337search2

That's impressive infrastructure.

But for us **right now it is overkill**.

SLIM becomes interesting if one day we have:

```text
10,000 agents

running across
multiple cloud providers

across multiple companies

communicating directly

with strong identity/security requirements
```

Then I'd revisit it.

For six specialist marketing agents inside one client's environment?

No.

---

# What about AutoGen?

AutoGen Core is explicitly an event-driven framework for scalable, distributed multi-agent systems, including distributed runtimes. citeturn472000search2

So yes, we could build:

```text
Researcher
   ↓ message bus
Strategist
   ↓
Growth
```

with AutoGen.

But then we'd have:

```text
Harness
+
LangGraph
+
AutoGen
```

and all three want to participate in:

state, orchestration, agents, events, messaging and lifecycle.

That would make the architecture worse.

AutoGen would make sense as a **replacement** for part of our stack, not an addition.

---

# Same issue with CrewAI

CrewAI has:

agents, crews, tasks, processes, delegation, sequential/hierarchical workflows, memory, state and flows. citeturn782013search0turn782013search1

In other words, it already implements:

```text
Manager
 │
 ├── Researcher
 ├── Writer
 └── Analyst

Tasks
Dependencies
Delegation
Processes
```

Very relevant conceptually.

But it's basically trying to own the same layer as:

```text
Harness + LangGraph + our Work Layer
```

Adding CrewAI would therefore be **duplication**, not infrastructure reuse.

Again: legitimate alternative architecture, poor additional dependency.

---

# Microsoft now has an interesting alternative too

Microsoft Agent Framework has become quite substantial. It includes agents, a harness, graph-based workflows, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop and built-in multi-agent patterns including sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat and manager-style coordination. citeturn123401search8turn123401search11

For example, Microsoft's handoff orchestration explicitly supports agents handing full task ownership to specialists, while its “agent as tool” pattern keeps a primary agent responsible and delegates only subtasks. citeturn123401search2

That's actually very close to decisions we're making.

But again, this tells me:

> Microsoft Agent Framework is a possible **alternative to Harness + LangGraph**.

It doesn't tell me we should add Microsoft Agent Framework *on top of them*.

That would be four frameworks managing agents.

---

# So I would make one change to our architecture

Instead of building a completely proprietary agent-work protocol, use:

> **A2A concepts as the generic foundation, plus our marketing-specific extensions.**

For instance:

```text
GENERIC WORK
────────────────────

Task
Message
Artifact
Status
Agent
Context

        +

OUR DOMAIN LANGUAGE
────────────────────

Evidence
Observation
Insight
Hypothesis
Recommendation
Decision
Experiment
BrandChange
Campaign
```

Then a task could be:

```text
Task

id:
task_481

agent:
researcher

skill:
competitor-analysis

status:
working

context:
positioning-project-42

input:
BoxRefs [...]

artifacts:
[]
```

and later:

```text
Artifact

type:
CompetitiveEvidencePackage

producer:
researcher

evidence_refs:
[...]

findings:
[...]

confidence:
0.88
```

That's very close to A2A already. citeturn841607search0

We then add our richer domain semantics.

---

# Our own coordination layer becomes tiny

Instead of building an “agent operating system”, we build essentially:

```text
              OUR WORK LAYER

Task
Artifact
Event
Dependency
Decision
BoxReference
        │
        ▼
     Postgres
```

And adapters:

```text
WorkTask
   │
   ├──→ Harness subagent request
   │
   ├──→ LangGraph run
   │
   ├──→ Feed event
   │
   └──→ A2A Task
```

That's exactly the kind of **small elegant adapter layer** you've been aiming for.

---

# The architecture would then have three communication mechanisms

And I think this separation is particularly clean:

```text
               OUR SYSTEM

AGENT ↔ TOOL
────────────────────
MCP

Researcher → web
Growth → HubSpot
Strategist → Box

INTERNAL AGENT ↔ AGENT
────────────────────
Harness

Director → Researcher
Researcher → Director
Strategist → Brand Guardian

EXTERNAL AGENT ↔ AGENT
────────────────────
A2A

Our Marketing OS → Salesforce Agent
Our Marketing OS → client's Finance Agent
External Agent → our Strategist
```

This actually matches the standards' intended boundaries: A2A is explicitly agent-to-agent interoperability, while MCP is agent-to-tool/context interoperability. citeturn841607search1

---

# And one shared Work Model sits above all of them

```text
                   WORK MODEL
                       │
         Task / Artifact / Event
                       │
       ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
       ▼               ▼               ▼

    Harness          LangGraph          A2A
   internal           reasoning        external
 communication         work          communication
```

That is where I think we've landed on something quite elegant.

## So: use another system or build light ourselves?

My answer is now:

**Do both, but at different levels.**

Don't invent communication transport, subagent sessions, distributed protocols or agent discovery.

Reuse:

**Harness** → internal agent runtime
**LangGraph** → reasoning orchestration
**A2A** → standard external agent protocol
**MCP** → tool protocol

But build a very small proprietary:

> **Marketing Work Model**

because that's where our useful semantics live.

And I would deliberately model its generic parts after A2A so that we don't paint ourselves into a corner.

I would **not add CrewAI, AutoGen, Microsoft Agent Framework or AGNTCY/SLIM now**. They mostly duplicate our current layers. I'd keep them in mind as replacements or scaling infrastructure if requirements change.

So the resulting system is actually getting simpler:

```text
KNOWLEDGE       Cognee
ANALYTICS       DuckDB
INTEGRATIONS    Nango
MODELS          LiteLLM

THINKING        LangGraph
AGENT RUNTIME   Harness
TOOLS           MCP
EXTERNAL AGENTS A2A

WORK SEMANTICS  OURS
INTELLIGENCE    OURS
PRODUCT         OURS
```

That feels like a much healthier boundary: **standards and open infrastructure underneath; our marketing intelligence and product semantics on top.** memcite

Yes. Looking back across the frontend direction we developed, I think the frontend is now quite well defined. And after checking the current ecosystem, **there is a lot we should reuse—but the distinctive feed + agent-character experience should remain ours.**

The key distinction is:

## What we had already converged on

The product started closer to a conventional Brand Core dashboard, but we moved away from that. The primary interface became a **private intelligence feed**, where the company’s specialist agents appear as persistent actors.

The home screen is essentially:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                 │
│  🔵 Researcher                                  │
│                                                 │
│  "Implementation friction appeared in 14 of    │
│   the latest 23 enterprise conversations."      │
│                                                 │
│  Evidence 14     Confidence 84%                 │
│                                                 │

│                                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                 │

│                                                 │

│                                                 │

│                                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

│  🟣 Storyteller                                 │
│                                                 │
│  "I developed three narrative territories..."  │
│                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

But the characters aren't emoji or generic robots. We settled on **abstract little creatures with distinct anatomy**, each agent having its own silhouette, color and movement vocabulary.

And an important visual rule emerged:

> **Avatar = expression**
> **UI = container**
> **Motion = meaning**

The UI itself stays quiet: neutral surfaces, restrained typography, minimal chrome and little decorative color. Almost all expressive color comes from the agents.

That means the frontend has two visual layers:

```text
CALM PRODUCT LAYER
────────────────────────
layout
cards
text
evidence
controls
navigation
data

EXPRESSIVE AGENT LAYER
────────────────────────
color
movement
personality
working state
energy
uncertainty
attention
```

I think that's still exactly the right direction. memcite

# The actual product surfaces we discussed

I would now formalize them like this:

| Surface | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Feed** | What matters right now |
| **Core** | What the system currently believes about the company |
| **Agents** | Who is working, what they're doing and what they've recently produced |
| **Work** | Projects, tasks, experiments and dependencies |
| **Library** | Research, creatives, campaigns, documents and generated artifacts |
| **History** | Decisions, belief changes, strategy changes and prior states |
| **Agent conversation** | Direct discussion with Researcher, Strategist, etc. |
| **Evidence view** | Drill from recommendation → insight → observations → original evidence |

The Feed remains the home screen.

Everything else is accessible by drilling down.

So:

```text
FEED POST

"Implementation speed appears
to be an emerging customer priority."

          ↓ click evidence

INSIGHT

18 supporting observations
confidence 0.81

          ↓

OBSERVATIONS

Sales call #27
Sales call #42
Customer survey #8
CRM pattern

          ↓

SOURCE

Original transcript
```

That progressive disclosure mirrors the progressive knowledge architecture we discussed for the Box.

---

# The feed itself should have typed posts

I wouldn't build it as arbitrary AI-generated HTML.

Our backend should emit a typed object such as:

```ts
FeedItem =
  | ObservationPost
  | InsightPost
  | HypothesisPost
  | RecommendationPost
  | ArtifactPost
  | QuestionPost
  | ResultPost
  | LearningPost
  | ExternalSignalPost
```

Then **we control exactly how each type renders**.

For example:

```text
ObservationPost
─────────────────
low-level discovery

InsightPost
─────────────────
synthesized meaning

HypothesisPost
─────────────────
uncertain interpretation

RecommendationPost
─────────────────
proposed decision/action

ResultPost
─────────────────
what happened

LearningPost
─────────────────
what the system learned
```

This is one of the frontend pieces we should definitely own.

---

# User interactions also have domain meaning

We had discussed:

```text
Like
Dislike
Comment
Ask
Save
Approve
Adjust
Share/tag
```

Those aren't merely UI buttons.

Their semantics feed back into the system.

For example:

```text
LIKE
→ weak preference signal

COMMENT
→ contextual signal

CORRECTION
→ strong epistemic signal

APPROVE
→ explicit decision

ADJUST
→ modify recommendation

REJECT
→ explicit negative decision
```

So the React button itself is trivial.

The meaning behind it is ours.

---

# The avatars should be actual state machines

We had settled on states roughly like:

```text
idle

thinking

searching

reading

comparing

connecting

synthesizing

creating

presenting

waiting_for_approval

success

uncertain

error
```

And those states should correspond to **real backend execution**, not random animation.

Example:

```text
LangGraph:
source_search

        ↓

Domain event:
research.searching

        ↓

Frontend:
Researcher state = SEARCHING

        ↓

Rive:
blue creature scans around
```

Then:

```text
LangGraph:
compare_evidence

        ↓

Researcher state = COMPARING

        ↓

avatar visually arranges
two objects side-by-side
```

This part is important because it makes the little guys a real **visualization of system state** rather than branding decoration.

---

# What I would reuse for the frontend

This is where the ecosystem is now quite good.

## Next.js + React + TypeScript

I would use **Next.js App Router** as the product shell.

It already gives us React Server Components, Suspense, Server Functions, layouts and the modern server/client boundary we need. citeturn981261search1

So:

```text
Next.js

/app/feed
/app/core
/app/agents
/app/work
/app/library
/app/history
```

No reason to invent web-app infrastructure.

---

# shadcn/ui + Radix for the boring UI

This is almost ideal for our aesthetic.

shadcn/ui deliberately gives you the **actual source code of components**, rather than locking you into a component-library package, so we can change every detail to match our design language. citeturn647156search0

Underneath, Radix gives us robust accessible primitives for things like dialogs, popovers, menus, tooltips, tabs and focus/keyboard management while remaining essentially unstyled. citeturn647156search1turn647156search2

That means we don't need to waste time implementing:

```text
dialog behavior
keyboard navigation
dropdowns
popovers
tooltips
selects
focus management
accessibility
```

while still being free to make everything look completely unlike standard shadcn.

I'd use it as **construction material**, not as our visual identity.

---

# assistant-ui for conversations

This is one of the strongest pieces I found for us.

I would **not** use assistant-ui for our Feed.

But I would absolutely consider it for:

```text
Agent chat
message composer
attachments
streaming
message actions
tool result rendering
approval widgets
thread behavior
```

Its primitives are deliberately headless/un-styled React building blocks that already handle streaming state, message composition, keyboard behavior, scrolling and tool calls. citeturn971416search0turn971416search2

So clicking:

```text
🟡 Strategist

[Discuss]
```

could open:

```text
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│ 🟡 Strategist                 │
│                               │
│ You                           │
│ Why do you think this is      │
│ strong enough to test?        │
│                               │
│ Strategist                    │
│ Three reasons...              │
│                               │
│ [evidence card]               │
│                               │
│ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Ask Strategist...         │ │
│ └───────────────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────┘
```

without us implementing the entire streaming-chat interaction model.

assistant-ui also has explicit support for rendering tool calls as custom interactive React components and human-interaction tools. citeturn971416search1turn971416search3

That fits things like:

```text
Strategist requests approval

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ Run positioning experiment │
│                            │
│ Estimated duration: 2 wks  │
│                            │
│ [Approve]      [Adjust]     │
└────────────────────────────┘
```

very nicely.

---

# The really interesting new addition: AG-UI

This is the frontend equivalent of MCP/A2A.

We already have:

```text
MCP
Agent ↔ Tools

A2A
Agent ↔ External Agents
```

I would seriously consider adding:

```text
AG-UI
Agent ↔ User Interface
```

AG-UI is an open event protocol specifically for agent-to-frontend communication. It covers run lifecycle, streamed text, tool calls, synchronized state, ongoing activity, human interaction and custom events. citeturn971416search8turn351746search4

This could save us from inventing our own WebSocket/event protocol.

Our architecture becomes:

```text
                BACKEND

        Harness + LangGraph
               │
               ▼
       Domain Event Adapter
               │
               ▼
             AG-UI
               │
       SSE / HTTP stream
               │
               ▼

               FRONTEND
```

AG-UI's JavaScript client already exposes event subscriptions, state tracking, aborting runs and an observable event stream. citeturn456618search0turn456618search1turn456618search2

---

# And AG-UI maps unusually well to our avatar concept

AG-UI now has **Activity events** specifically designed for ongoing activity/progress, along with state snapshot/delta events. citeturn351746search0

So we could translate:

```text
Harness event
tool: web_search

        ↓

our domain translator

ResearcherSearching

        ↓

AG-UI ActivitySnapshot

{
  agent: "researcher",
  state: "searching",
  query: "enterprise SaaS implementation positioning"
}

        ↓

Frontend

ResearcherAvatar → searching
```

Then:

```text
ResearcherComparingEvidence
        ↓
AG-UI ActivityDelta
        ↓
avatar transitions
```

That's extremely close to what we were going to invent ourselves.

---

# AG-UI also lets us keep our custom domain vocabulary

It includes a `Custom` event specifically for application-defined semantics. citeturn351746search0turn351746search1

So we can still emit:

```text
insight.created

hypothesis.updated

recommendation.proposed

approval.required

evidence.added

decision.confirmed

task.assigned
```

without modifying the standard.

That's exactly the right architecture.

---

# I would not necessarily use CopilotKit

CopilotKit is heavily invested in AG-UI and provides React components, shared state, generative UI and human-in-the-loop functionality. It already integrates with LangGraph and many other agent frameworks. citeturn404960search0turn404960search9

It's good infrastructure.

But for **our** product I suspect it does slightly too much.

Our UI is not primarily:

> “embed an AI copilot into an app.”

The entire application **is the AI organization**.

I'd rather use:

```text
@ag-ui/core
@ag-ui/client
+
our React UI
```

and selectively use assistant-ui for conversations.

That gives us more aesthetic/product control.

---

# Motion for the product UI

For normal interface movement—cards entering the feed, opening detail views, drawers, hovering, reordering, transitions—I'd use **Motion for React**.

Motion handles React-based layout animations, gestures, enter/exit transitions, springs and state-driven animations. citeturn362885search2turn362885search0

So:

```text
feed card enters
detail expands
post changes state
approval collapses
drawer opens
```

all use Motion.

But I would keep those animations restrained.

Remember:

> the UI itself should stay calm.

---

# Rive for the little guys

This is where I think **Rive is particularly suitable**.

Rive has actual visual state machines consisting of states, transitions, inputs and layers, and those state machines can be driven programmatically from the application runtime. citeturn362885search10turn362885search3

That means each agent avatar could literally contain:

```text
Researcher.riv

StateMachine:

IDLE
SEARCHING
READING
COMPARING
CONNECTING
SYNTHESIZING
PRESENTING
WAITING
SUCCESS
UNCERTAIN
ERROR
```

Our React component just says:

```text
<AgentAvatar
    agent="researcher"
    state="comparing"
/>
```

Rive handles the visual transition.

That's much better than implementing complex character animation manually with CSS.

So I would divide motion:

```text
Motion
→ interface movement

Rive
→ character movement
```

Very clean.

---

# TanStack Query for durable frontend data

Our Feed, Core, Work, Library and History are not primarily LLM streams.

They are ordinary **server state**.

TanStack Query is designed around fetching, caching, synchronizing and updating asynchronous server state, including integration with Next.js server rendering. citeturn647156search4turn647156search12

So I would have:

```text
TanStack Query
─────────────────

feed
core entities
tasks
projects
artifacts
history
agents
comments
decisions
```

while:

```text
AG-UI
─────────────────

active agent run
streaming
tool activity
live state
avatar activity
interrupts
live result generation
```

That's an important separation.

---

# Durable feed versus live activity

I would not make AG-UI itself the database.

Imagine Researcher is working:

```text
LIVE
──────────────────────────

Researcher is searching...
Researcher is comparing...
Researcher is synthesizing...
```

Those can be transient AG-UI activity events.

When it has something worth saying:

```text
DURABLE
──────────────────────────

InsightCreated
        ↓
Postgres Work/Feed store
        ↓
FeedItem #829
```

Then the frontend updates its TanStack Query cache.

So:

```text
       AGENT RUN

           │

       AG-UI events
           │
           ▼
    live avatar/activity

           │
      meaningful result
           ▼

       WORK LEDGER
        Postgres
           │
           ▼
        FEED ITEM
           │
           ▼
   TanStack Query cache
```

This prevents our feed from becoming a replay of raw agent logs.

---

Most of the normal frontend machinery disappears.

But the **important product layer remains ours**.

| Component | Build or reuse? |

| React framework | Next.js |
| Accessible primitives | Radix/shadcn |
| Styling foundation | Tailwind/CSS |
| Server-state caching | TanStack Query |

| **Feed architecture** | **OURS** |

| **Agent avatar designs** | **OURS** |
| **Avatar state vocabulary** | **OURS** |
| **Harness/LangGraph → domain event mapping** | **OURS** |
| **Core explorer** | **OURS** |
| **Evidence drilldown** | **OURS** |
| **Work view** | **OURS** |
| **Interaction semantics** | **OURS** |
| **Approval/rejection UX** | mostly ours on primitives |
| **Agent identity/personality UI** | **OURS** |
| **History visualization** | **OURS** |

That's a very favorable split.

# There is one frontend adapter we definitely need

Something approximately like:

```text
Harness / LangGraph
        ↓
Runtime events
        ↓
──────────────────────────────
   OUR UI EVENT TRANSLATOR
──────────────────────────────
        ↓
AG-UI
        ↓
Frontend
```

For example:

```text
raw Harness:

tool/call web.search
```

becomes:

```text
domain:

research.search_started
```

then:

```text
AG-UI:

ActivitySnapshot
```

then:

```text
React:

agentActivityStore["researcher"]
    = SEARCHING
```

then:

```text
Rive:

Researcher.searching
```

This is probably only a modest amount of code, but architecturally it's important because **we don't want the frontend coupled directly to Harness internals**.

---

# And the same translator produces feed events

```text
LangGraph:
strategic_recommendation node finished

          ↓

Domain translator

RecommendationCreated

          ↓

Postgres

          ↓

FeedItem

          ↓

Frontend

<RecommendationPost />
```

So frontend never asks:

> “What is LangGraph node 8?”

It understands:

> “The Strategist created a recommendation.”

That's exactly the abstraction we want.

---

# I would not use generative UI everywhere

Both assistant-ui and current agent-UI ecosystems can let models dynamically choose/render UI components. assistant-ui supports constrained generative UI from a component allowlist as well as LangGraph-emitted UI. citeturn971416search11turn741323search5

Useful occasionally.

But I would **not** let agents dynamically design the main feed.

Our product should have extremely consistent interaction grammar.

The model can decide:

```text
Recommendation
Evidence
Question
Experiment
```

but **we decide how Recommendation looks**.

This keeps the interface elegant and predictable.

---

# What I would not add

I don't think we need a large dashboard framework, Material UI-style visual system, generic admin template, another frontend-agent runtime, elaborate global-state framework, or real-time collaboration product at V1.

Those would either fight our design language or duplicate AG-UI/TanStack/assistant-ui.

Similarly, AI SDK UI is good infrastructure for streaming chat and tool calls and can work with custom backends, but if we adopt **AG-UI + assistant-ui**, much of its frontend role would overlap. citeturn981261search9turn981261search12

So I wouldn't automatically add it.

---
